tagline: From Zero to Fluent in AI

modules.title: What Even Is AI?
modules.subtitle: A crisp 5-minute foundation: how modern AI works, which model to pick, and what chat apps hide under the hood.

chapters.title: Rules vs. Patterns: Why AI Feels Different
chapters.summary: Regular software obeys exact rules written by programmers. Modern AI learns fuzzy patterns from millions of examples—making it great at messy language and unreliable at exact math.

analogy.title: The Tax Table vs. The Experienced Editor
analogy.body: A spreadsheet formula is regular software: give it the same numbers and it returns the exact same total every time. Modern AI is more like a seasoned editor who has read ten thousand memos—it cannot prove a math formula, yet it spots tone, structure, and awkward phrasing immediately.

sections.heading: Regular software follows exact recipes
sections.body: Calculators, spreadsheets, and banking systems run on explicit rules written in advance: if a balance drops below zero, trigger an alert. Whenever a task demands 100% repeatable accuracy, hand-written rules are still undefeated.

callout.title: Where rigid rules break down
callout.body: Try writing fixed rules to flag rude customer emails. Blocking a list of bad words misses polite sarcasm ("Thanks for wasting my afternoon") and wrongly flags harmless messages.

sections.heading: AI learns patterns into frozen weights
sections.body: Instead of hand-coding rules, AI labs train a network on billions of examples, adjusting internal numbers called **model weights** until its guesses improve. That expensive study phase is **training**. When you send a prompt later, the weights stay frozen while it generates a reply—a fast step called **inference**.

callout.title: Your chat does not retrain the model
callout.body: Sending a message runs inference on frozen weights. Your prompt may shape the current thread, yet it does not rewrite the model’s core knowledge in real time.

sections.heading: Pick the right tool for the job
sections.body: Because AI predicts probabilities rather than running exact formulas, reach for it on messy human tasks—drafting replies, summarizing notes, comparing options, or untangling jargon. Keep exact arithmetic, budgets, and legal totals inside spreadsheets or deterministic code.

callout.title: Best combo: AI writes the formula, software runs it
callout.body: Need to sum 500 expense rows by category? Ask AI to write the spreadsheet formula, then let the spreadsheet calculate the exact number.

keyTakeaways: Regular software executes exact human-written rules; AI applies statistical patterns learned from examples.
Training tunes model weights upfront; everyday prompting runs inference on frozen weights.
Use AI for messy language and drafting, and deterministic software for exact calculations.

quiz.question: How does modern AI handle a messy task like sorting sarcastic customer complaints differently from traditional software?
options: It looks up every complaint against a live database maintained by human moderators.
It learns statistical patterns from examples instead of relying on fixed rules.
It automatically rewrites its source code line by line after every customer email.
It converts every sentence into a strict yes-or-no spreadsheet formula before replying.
quiz.explanation: Traditional software relies on explicit rules written by humans, whereas modern AI learns flexible patterns across huge sets of examples.

quiz.question: When you correct a mistake in a chat with Claude or ChatGPT, the model permanently updates its core weights for all users right away.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. Chatting runs inference on frozen model weights. Your correction only helps inside that active conversation unless a separate training run happens later.

quiz.question: Maya pastes 600 monthly receipts into a plain AI chat and asks for an exact tax total instead of using a spreadsheet. What is the real risk?
options: Spreadsheets cannot categorize receipts without an AI plugin.
AI chat models refuse to process messages that contain currency symbols or decimals.
Probabilistic language models can miscount exact arithmetic across long lists.
Pasting financial numbers into a chat automatically retrains the model weights overnight.
quiz.explanation: Language models estimate plausible text rather than running a calculator on every row. Let AI draft the spreadsheet formula, and let the spreadsheet sum the exact total.

chapters.title: How LLMs Write: One Token at a Time
chapters.summary: A Large Language Model does not retrieve stored answers from a vault. It builds every reply fresh by predicting the next chunk of text—which explains both its creativity and its confident mistakes.

analogy.title: Phone Autocomplete Scaled to an Entire Library
analogy.body: When your phone keyboard suggests "tomorrow" after "See you", it is predicting the next likely word. An LLM does the same thing after studying vast amounts of writing and code—so predicting the next chunk accurately requires capturing grammar, logic, and structure.

sections.heading: What "Large Language Model" means in plain English
sections.body: **Large** refers to billions of tuned weights trained on massive text collections. **Language** reflects how it reads and writes human prose and code—and modern **multimodal** models also take screenshots, photos, or audio as input. **Model** simply means a mathematical map of patterns.

callout.title: Why next-chunk guessing looks like reasoning
callout.body: To predict the next piece after "A $40 shirt with 25% off costs $", the model must pick "30"—meaning training quietly rewards patterns that track math, logic, and context.

sections.heading: Generated live, never copied from an answer vault
sections.body: An LLM writes one small text chunk (**token**) at a time, feeds that chunk back into the conversation, and predicts the next until it outputs a stop signal. Because several continuations can have similar probabilities, asking the same creative prompt twice often yields two fresh answers.

callout.title: Fluent tone does not prove a fact is real
callout.body: Post-training teaches models to sound clear and helpful, not to verify every fact. Without a live search tool or a source you paste in, a model can smoothly invent a realistic quote or citation.

sections.heading: Reading the clues when an answer feels off
sections.body: Once you know replies are predicted sequentially, three everyday quirks make total sense: models stream word by word, they can change phrasing on a retry, and they need **grounding** (real documents or web search) whenever accuracy on recent or niche facts matters.

callout.title: Spot ungrounded claims fast
callout.body: Whenever an AI gives you a specific date, price, law, or link from memory alone, treat it as a draft to verify—not a verified lookup.

keyTakeaways: LLMs generate every reply sequentially via next-token prediction rather than pulling saved scripts from a database.
Multimodal models extend the same pattern engine to screenshots, photos, PDFs, and audio.
Polished prose is a product of pattern prediction and post-training—always verify ungrounded facts.

quiz.question: Why does asking the exact same brainstorming prompt twice often give you two different replies?
options: The model samples among probable next tokens as it generates each reply fresh.
The server switches you to another AI company on retries.
The model checks your past browser cookies to intentionally avoid repeating earlier words.
Each reply is picked randomly from a fixed list of pre-written responses saved by engineers.
quiz.explanation: LLMs generate replies token by token from probability distributions. For open-ended prompts, multiple tokens are plausible, so fresh runs naturally vary.

quiz.question: Because a multimodal LLM can read a screenshot of a receipt or error screen, it automatically searches the live internet to verify every detail in the image.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False. Being multimodal only means the model can process images alongside text. Live internet verification still requires an external search tool.

quiz.question: Daniel asks an offline AI model for the closing price of a stock today and concludes: "It gave me a specific number with two decimals, so it must have checked live market data." What is the mistake?
options: Offline models are unable to format numbers with decimal places unless connected to Excel.
Stock prices are updated only once a week, so the model could have remembered them from training.
Next-token prediction can generate a fluent, plausible number even without live web access.
Only multimodal models with camera permissions are allowed to read financial websites.
quiz.explanation: A bare LLM has frozen knowledge and optimizes for plausible continuations. Unless a wrapper explicitly runs a live search tool, specific numbers about today can be pure guesses.

chapters.title: Choosing a Model: Families, Tiers & Open Weights
chapters.summary: Not all AI is one brain. Major labs ship fast, balanced, and reasoning tiers—and open-weights models let people run AI privately without depending on a single cloud vendor.

analogy.title: Hatchbacks, Sedans, and Heavy Trucks
analogy.body: Calling every AI "ChatGPT" is like calling every vehicle a sedan. Different makers build separate model families, and each maker sells nimble economy tiers for quick errands alongside heavy-duty thinkers for tough problems.

sections.heading: Separate builders, distinct strengths
sections.body: Three hosted cloud families dominate everyday apps: **Claude** (Anthropic), **Gemini** (Google), and **GPT** (OpenAI). They are trained independently by rival teams, so their writing tone, context limits, tool integrations, and pricing all differ.

callout.title: Match the tier to the task
callout.body: Fast/mini tiers shine on proofreading, translations, and quick summaries. Save slower flagship or reasoning tiers for complex plans, subtle debugging, or high-stakes analysis.

sections.heading: Open-weights models change who controls the model
sections.body: Teams such as Meta (**Llama**), **DeepSeek**, **Qwen**, and **Mistral** release **open-weights** models—publishing the finished parameter files publicly. Anyone can host them on chosen servers or run compact versions directly on their own hardware offline.

callout.title: When private or local matters
callout.body: Summarizing personal medical notes or sensitive journal drafts on an offline device keeps every word off third-party cloud servers and costs nothing per message.

sections.heading: Skip benchmark obsession
sections.body: Leaderboard charts change every month and rarely predict how useful a model feels on your real tasks. In daily life, giving crisp context and checking outputs improves results far more than chasing the newest model name.

callout.title: More expensive does not always mean better for the job
callout.body: Sending a grocery list to a slow flagship reasoning model wastes time and money when a fast small tier finishes the same job cleanly in half a second.

keyTakeaways: Claude, Gemini, and GPT are separate model families built by independent labs—not one shared backend.
Use fast small tiers for quick routine tasks and heavier reasoning tiers only when complexity justifies the wait and cost.
Open-weights models publish their trained weights so you can self-host or run compact versions privately offline.

quiz.question: Which task is the BEST fit for a fast, smaller model tier instead of a slow flagship reasoning model?
options: Auditing a tangled multi-file payment bug with subtle race conditions across a whole app.
Designing a long-term database migration strategy with strict rollback constraints.
Cleaning up typos and bullet formatting in ten lines of meeting notes.
Comparing conflicting legal clauses across three dense commercial supplier contracts.
quiz.explanation: Fast small tiers handle routine formatting, proofreading, and simple rewrites in a split second at a fraction of the cost—reserve heavy reasoning models for genuinely hard problems.

quiz.question: An open-weights model publishes its trained weight files so individuals or companies can host or run it on hardware they control.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True. Publishing the trained parameter files lets people run open-weights models on private servers or personal devices instead of relying on a single vendor’s cloud.

quiz.question: A colleague says: "I switched from ChatGPT to Claude and Gemini, so I am just paying three apps to talk to the exact same model underneath." What did they get wrong?
options: Claude, Gemini, and GPT are distinct model families trained separately by Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI.
ChatGPT and Gemini share identical weights, while only Claude runs on an open-weights engine.
All three websites run locally on your phone hardware without calling any cloud servers.
The underlying models are identical, and only the app color themes and login screens differ.
quiz.explanation: Each lab trains its own model family with its own architecture, training mix, context limits, and pricing—they are genuinely different models, not reskins of one engine.

chapters.title: Raw Models vs. AI Apps: What the Wrapper Adds
chapters.summary: A raw AI model only takes input and outputs text—with zero memory between turns. Everything else you see in ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini comes from the app wrapped around it.

analogy.title: A Bare Engine vs. A Finished Car
analogy.body: A raw LLM is like an engine sitting on a workshop stand: powerful, yet unable to steer or brake by itself. A chat app bolts on the seats, fuel gauge, GPS, and steering wheel so you can actually drive.

sections.heading: Raw models start every request with amnesia
sections.body: By itself, a raw model has no saved history, no file browser, and no live web access. It is **stateless**: each call starts blank. When a chat app seems to remember message #1 during message #6, the app is quietly bundling and resending messages #1 through #6 together.

callout.title: Why mega-long chats lose track
callout.body: Because every turn resends earlier history into a fixed memory limit, endless rambling threads eventually crowd out early instructions and make replies slower and less focused.

sections.heading: What the chat wrapper quietly adds
sections.body: Consumer chat apps layer four big features around the raw model: **saved history**, a hidden **system prompt** (date, style, safety rules), **built-in tools** (web search, file readers, calculators), and a polished interface for streaming replies.

callout.title: Same model, two different answers
callout.body: Ask a bare API model for today’s train delays and it declines. Ask the exact same model inside a chat app with web search turned on, and the wrapper fetches live results first.

sections.heading: One seam explains the entire AI ecosystem
sections.body: Once you separate the **raw model** from the **wrapper**, every AI product clicks into place. Voice assistants, research apps, and coding agents simply wrap the same raw models with different instructions and tools—setting you up for tokens, APIs, and agents in Units 2–4.

callout.title: Check what tools are turned on
callout.body: Before blaming a model for missing a live fact or file, check whether the app you are using actually has web search or file access enabled.

keyTakeaways: Raw LLMs are stateless: they accept input and return text with no built-in chat memory or live internet.
Chat apps are wrappers that resend conversation history, inject hidden system instructions, and attach tools like web search.
Seeing the split between model and wrapper explains how chatbots, search assistants, and coding agents all work.

quiz.question: When you ask a follow-up question on turn #6 of a mobile AI chat, how does the AI know what you asked on turn #1?
options: The raw model permanently memorizes each user’s account history inside its frozen weights.
Your phone operating system caches the model’s internal weights between every message.
The chat app stores the thread and resends the earlier turns along with your new message.
The AI runs a live web search on your profile name to reconstruct the earlier messages.
quiz.explanation: Raw models are stateless. The wrapper app saves your conversation and sends the prior turns back to the model with every new message.

quiz.question: Two apps can call the exact same underlying AI model yet give different capabilities if one app attaches web search and file tools while the other does not.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True. Capabilities like live search, document reading, and saved memory come from the wrapper around the model, not from the bare weights alone.

quiz.question: Priya tests a bare model via API and gets "I cannot check live cricket scores," even though the same provider’s mobile app answered right away. She assumes the API runs an older, weaker model. What did she miss?
options: Mobile apps always run a private model withheld from API developers.
The mobile app wraps the model with a live web-search tool that a bare API call lacks.
Sports scores stay blocked on API accounts until you buy a subscription.
Bare API calls can only return code snippets, never everyday facts.
quiz.explanation: It can be the exact same model underneath—the consumer app automatically attaches a web-search tool, whereas a bare API call only uses tools you explicitly connect.

masteryCheck.title: Unit 1 Mastery Check
masteryCheck.subtitle: Four quick real-world scenarios to prove you can tell models, apps, and tools apart.

questions.question: You have 450 invoice lines to total for a client tax report and a tense client email to soften. What is the smartest split between regular software and AI?
options: Use AI for both tasks so the invoice math matches the tone of the apology email.
Let a spreadsheet sum the invoices and use AI to draft the email.
Write custom spreadsheet macros to draft the apology email and let AI add the numbers.
Ask a flagship reasoning model to sum all 450 rows twice and average its two replies.
questions.explanation: Deterministic spreadsheets guarantee 100% accurate arithmetic, while LLMs shine on messy human tone and phrasing.

questions.question: An offline AI model gives a confident, well-formatted paragraph quoting a 2026 court ruling you never heard of. A teammate says: "It wrote an exact case number and date, so it must be real." What is the mistake?
options: Next-token prediction can fabricate fluent citations without real verification.
Offline models only cite real cases if you prompt in lowercase.
Post-training removes all legal knowledge unless a paid cloud subscription stays active.
Case numbers are reliable when the model answers quickly.
questions.explanation: LLMs generate plausible-looking continuations token by token. Fluent formatting and exact numbers never prove a fact—verify ungrounded claims against real sources.

questions.question: A clinic wants to summarize private patient intake notes completely offline without sending text to any external cloud vendor. Which option fits best?
options: Switching a hosted chat app to dark mode with search off.
Using the largest hosted cloud flagship model because expensive tiers never log prompts.
Running a compact open-weights model locally on hardware the clinic controls.
Asking a web chatbot to promise at the top of the prompt that it will delete the weights.
questions.explanation: Open-weights models publish their trained weights so organizations and individuals can host or run them privately on their own hardware with zero cloud transmission.

questions.question: After 40 turns in one mobile chat, an AI forgets a rule you gave in message #1. Your friend blames the AI for "losing its training." What actually explains it?
options: Consumer apps erase the model’s training weights once a chat passes thirty messages.
Your phone automatically switches from an LLM to regular software after half an hour.
The model permanently forgets message #1 unless you upgrade to an open-weights tier.
Raw models are stateless, and the chat wrapper’s resending history crowded out early context.
questions.explanation: The model’s weights never changed during inference—the wrapper app resends prior turns on each message, and long threads eventually crowd out or dilute early rules.

modules.title: Tokens, Context & Talking to AI
modules.subtitle: Learn how AI slices your text, why it forgets long chats, and how to prompt cleanly.

chapters.title: What Are Tokens? Why AI Reads Chunks, Not Letters
chapters.summary: AI does not read English letter by letter or even strictly word by word. Before a model sees your message, a tokenizer chops it into bite-sized numbered pieces called tokens.

analogy.title: Lego Bricks of Language
analogy.body: Imagine building sentences out of Lego bricks instead of individual letters. Common everyday words like "house" or "coffee" come as a single pre-molded brick. Less common words like "unbelievable" snap together from three smaller bricks: "un" + "believ" + "able". Every AI model reads, counts, and charges by the brick.

sections.heading: Why AI uses tokens instead of letters or whole words
sections.body:
Computers only understand numbers, so every piece of text has to be turned into numbers before an AI can process it. If we numbered every single letter (a=1, b=2), sentences would turn into super long chains that are slow to read. If we numbered every possible word in every language plus typos and code names, the dictionary would explode to millions of entries.

Tokens are the sweet spot in the middle. A program called a tokenizer keeps a vocabulary of roughly 50,000 to 200,000 common word pieces. In everyday English, **1 token equals roughly ¾ of a word**—so 100 tokens is about 75 words, and a 300-word email is around 400 tokens.

callout.title: Why AI sometimes miscounts the "r"s in "strawberry"
callout.body: Because the tokenizer hands the model chunks like ["str", "aw", "berry"] represented as ID numbers—not individual spelled-out letters—counting letters inside a chunk feels like counting how many bricks are inside a sealed box without opening it!

sections.heading: Spaces, emojis, code, and other languages cost different tokens
sections.body:
Not all characters cost the same number of tokens. Punctuation, blank spaces, and leading spaces often attach right onto the start of a word token. Meanwhile, emojis, complex code symbols, and non-English scripts (like Hindi, Tamil, Arabic, or Japanese) frequently split into 2 to 4 tokens per word or symbol.

That means two messages that look the same length on screen can use very different token counts under the hood.

callout.title: Quick mental check: estimate tokens on your phone
callout.body: Picture four inputs side by side: `"coffee"` is **1 token**, `"unbelievable"` splits into **3 tokens** (`un` + `believ` + `able`), a single emoji like `🚀` can take **2–3 tokens**, and a 75-word text message lands right around **100 tokens**.

sections.heading: Three everyday reasons tokens matter to you
sections.body:
You never need to count tokens manually, yet knowing they exist immediately clears up three common mysteries:

1. **Speed**: Generating 1,000 tokens takes roughly twice as long as generating 500 tokens because the model creates one token at a time.
2. **Memory limits**: Every AI has a maximum token budget per conversation (its context window).
3. **Cost**: When you use pay-as-you-go API credits in Unit 3, providers bill per million tokens—not per message or per minute.

callout.title: Myth Buster: "One token = one word"
callout.body: Close, but not exact! Short common words like "cat" are 1 token, long words like "extraordinary" are 2–3 tokens, and messy URLs or emojis can burn through tokens surprisingly fast.

keyTakeaways: A token is a chunk of text (roughly ¾ of an English word) that AI models read, generate, and measure.
A tokenizer converts your text into numbered tokens going in and converts the model’s numbered tokens back into readable words coming out.
Tokens explain why AI occasionally struggles with spelling puzzles, why longer replies take longer, and how AI pricing works.

quiz.question: Roughly how many everyday English words correspond to 100 tokens?
options: Roughly 25 English words
Roughly 200 English words
Roughly 75 English words
Exactly 100 English words
quiz.explanation: In typical English text, 1 token is roughly ¾ of a word—so 100 tokens works out to around 75 words.

quiz.question: An emoji or a word in a non-English language can sometimes use more than one token.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True! Tokenizers optimize common English words into single tokens, while emojis, special symbols, and less-frequent scripts often split into 2–4 tokens.

quiz.question: Sam thinks: "My AI miscounted the letters in strawberry, which proves it is bad at all logic and coding." What is the real explanation?
options: Models ignore lowercase letters unless separated by hyphens.
Tokenizers feed models numbered word-chunks rather than individual letters.
Spelling puzzles need live search because dictionaries are excluded.
Modern LLMs only process whole sentences at once and cannot inspect anything shorter than a word.
quiz.explanation: Letter-counting quirks come from how tokenizers chunk text into multi-letter pieces before the model even sees them—not from an inability to reason.

chapters.title: The Context Window: AI’s Working Desk
chapters.summary: Every AI model has a fixed "working desk" called its context window. Understanding how that desk fills up explains why super long chats get sluggish, pricey, or forgetful—and how to keep them sharp.

analogy.title: Papers on a Working Desk
analogy.body: Picture an analyst sitting at a desk of fixed size. Every instruction you give, every PDF you attach, every back-and-forth message, and every reply the AI writes is another sheet of paper spread across that desk. Once the desk is covered edge to edge, sliding a brand-new sheet onto the front pushes the oldest sheet off the back—out of sight and completely forgotten.

sections.heading: What actually sits inside the context window?
sections.body:
Beginners often think the context window only counts the single message they just typed. In reality, it holds **everything** active in that conversation at once:

• Hidden system instructions and tool descriptions
• Files, screenshots, or code snippets you attached
• Every previous message you sent in this thread
• Every previous reply the AI generated
• The new answer the AI is about to write right now

callout.title: How big are modern context windows?
callout.body: Early AI models had tiny 4,000-token desks (about 6 pages). Today’s models commonly offer 128,000 to 200,000 tokens (a thick 400-page book), and some Gemini models stretch up to 1,000,000+ tokens!

sections.heading: Why a cluttered desk still hurts quality
sections.body:
Even if your model boasts a massive 200,000-token desk, piling 80 unrelated topics onto one endless chat thread causes "context rot." Just like a human trying to focus at a messy desk buried in old receipts, the AI can get distracted by dead-end ideas or outdated drafts you abandoned twenty messages ago.

Even worse, because the app re-sends the whole desk on every turn, a bloated chat gets slower and uses far more tokens on every single message.

callout.title: Start a fresh chat when switching topics
callout.body: Finished planning your weekend trip and now want help writing a resume? Tap "New Chat"! A clean desk gives faster, smarter, and cheaper answers.

sections.heading: Keeping long projects crisp without losing your work
sections.body:
What if you are working on one big project—like planning an event or designing a site—and your chat gets really long? You have two pro moves:

1. **Summarize and restart**: Ask the AI, "Summarize all our agreed decisions and current progress in 8 bullet points," copy that crisp summary, and paste it into a brand-new chat.
2. **Use `/compact`**: Modern AI coding tools include a built-in `/compact` command that tidies up the desk for you automatically.

callout.title: Watch out for silent forgetting
callout.body: When a conversation overflows the context window, the AI usually will not shout "I forgot message #1!" It quietly stops seeing the earliest messages—so if it suddenly ignores a rule you set an hour ago, your desk is probably full.

keyTakeaways: The context window is the maximum total tokens an AI can keep on its working desk at once (instructions + files + full chat history + new reply).
Once the context window fills up, older messages get dropped or summarized, causing the AI to forget earlier details.
Starting fresh chats for new topics—or summarizing progress into a clean thread—keeps AI sharper, faster, and cheaper.

quiz.question: Which items count toward a model’s context window on turn 10 of a conversation?
options: System instructions, attached files, all prior turns, and the new reply.
Only the newest message you typed plus any PDF or image uploaded on that turn.
Only the AI’s previous answers, since user prompts are compressed out after turn one.
Everything in your account’s entire chat sidebar across all past conversations.
quiz.explanation: Everything active in the current thread counts together: hidden instructions, attached files, all prior back-and-forth turns, and the reply currently being generated.

quiz.question: Keeping one giant 300-message chat thread for every unrelated question all month is the best way to get sharp answers.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Unrelated old messages clutter the context window, distract the model, slow responses down, and burn extra tokens. Open a fresh chat for new topics!

quiz.question: Maya uploaded 40 pages of notes and chatted for two hours. Suddenly the AI ignores a formatting rule she gave in message #1. She thinks it is deliberately ignoring her. What likely happened?
options: The model automatically resets its formatting rules every thirty minutes for privacy reasons.
Uploading PDF notes switches the model into read-only mode where formatting instructions stop working.
The provider quietly downgraded her chat mid-thread to a smaller model that cannot follow lists.
The long thread diluted or pushed message #1 out of active context; a fresh thread with a brief summary restores focus.
quiz.explanation: Long threads dilute or push out early rules. Summarizing your key decisions into a clean new thread (or running `/compact` in CLI tools) restores laser focus.

chapters.title: System Prompts, User Prompts & Temperature
chapters.summary: Great results come less from "secret magic prompts" and more from clear roles, concrete context, and knowing how the creativity dial (temperature) shapes replies.

analogy.title: The Director’s Brief vs. The Scene Line
analogy.body: Imagine filming a movie. The System Prompt is the director’s overall brief handed to the actor before cameras roll ("You play a calm, empathetic family doctor who speaks in simple everyday words"). The User Prompt is the specific line the patient says in that scene ("My knee clicks when I climb stairs"). Temperature is how much improvisation the director allows.

sections.heading: System prompt vs. User prompt: two layers of instruction
sections.body:
Almost every AI conversation has two distinct layers:

• **System Prompt**: Top-level standing rules that set the AI’s persona, tone, format, and boundaries for the entire session. In apps you build (or tools like Claude Code), you write this once so the AI remembers your style automatically.
• **User Prompt**: The specific request you type right now ("Draft a polite 3-sentence reply declining this meeting").

Separating standing rules from today’s task prevents you from repeating "keep it concise and jargon-free" twenty times a day.

callout.title: Vague prompt vs. Clear 4-part prompt
callout.body:
Vague: "Write an email about our workshop."
Clear: "Write a warm 120-word invite email (Goal) for non-technical small-business owners (Audience) announcing our free Saturday AI Basics workshop at 10 AM (Context). End with one bold RSVP link placeholder and no cheesy exclamation marks (Constraints)."

sections.heading: The 4 ingredients of a rock-solid prompt
sections.body:
You do not need to buy "500 secret prompt templates." Nearly every strong prompt simply answers four human questions:

1. **Goal**: What exact outcome do you want?
2. **Context / Audience**: Who is this for, and what background facts matter?
3. **Examples**: Show one sample of the tone or structure you love ("Match this style: ...").
4. **Constraints**: Word limit, format (bullet list, table, JSON), and what to avoid.

Bonus trick: if you are unsure what details matter, finish your prompt with **"Ask me 3 quick clarifying questions before you start."**

callout.title: Show, do not just tell
callout.body: Giving even ONE short example of what "good" looks like beats two paragraphs of abstract adjectives like "make it engaging, punchy, and modern."

sections.heading: Temperature: the predictability vs. creativity dial
sections.body:
Remember how an LLM assigns probabilities to every possible next token? **Temperature** is a numeric dial (commonly `0.0` to `1.0`) that decides whether the model sticks strictly to the top-ranked token or occasionally picks surprising runners-up.

• **Low temperature (0.0–0.2)**: Calm, steady, repeatable. Ideal for extracting invoice numbers, translating accurately, or editing code.
• **Medium temperature (0.4–0.7)**: Natural everyday conversation and clear explanations.
• **High temperature (0.8–1.0+)**: Playful, unexpected, diverse—great for brainstorming brand names or story twists (though too high turns into gibberish!).

callout.title: Myth Buster: Lowering temperature to 0 eliminates hallucinations
callout.body: Temperature 0 makes the AI pick its most predictable guess every time—which makes answers repeatable, NOT guaranteed true. If the model does not know a fact, its most predictable guess can still be confidently wrong!

keyTakeaways: System prompts set standing rules, role, and tone for a whole session; user prompts ask for today’s specific task.
Clear prompts cover four simple pieces: Goal, Context/Audience, Examples, and Constraints—no magic phrases required.
Temperature controls randomness: keep it low for precise, repeatable work and higher for creative brainstorming.

quiz.question: When should you prefer a LOW temperature setting (like 0.0–0.2)?
options: Brainstorming playful names for a new coffee roaster.
Generating several contrasting short-story endings so every retry feels surprising and fresh.
Extracting invoice dates or fixing a focused software bug.
Forcing the model to write longer multi-page essays with richer descriptive adjectives.
quiz.explanation: Low temperature keeps the AI steady and focused on the highest-probability tokens, which is ideal for structured extraction, math steps, and reliable code edits.

quiz.question: Setting temperature to 0 guarantees that an AI will never hallucinate or make factual mistakes.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Temperature 0 only makes output more consistent and predictable. If the AI lacks real facts, it can still repeat a plausible-sounding wrong guess.

quiz.question: Alex wants a landing page headline for his neighborhood bakery and types only: "Give me marketing copy." Why will the result feel generic?
options: Short prompts automatically trigger a weaker small model.
Missing audience, vibe, example, and length forces generic average phrasing.
Marketing copy needs a system prompt to specify brand tone.
Without setting temperature above 0.9, the model can only repeat standard dictionary definitions.
quiz.explanation: Vague inputs produce average generic outputs. Adding who the bakery serves, the vibe (cozy sourdough vs. luxury pastry), and a short length constraint transforms the result immediately.

chapters.title: Hallucinations: Why AI Sounds Confident When It’s Wrong
chapters.summary: AI does not lie out of malice—it invents plausible-sounding falsehoods because predicting smooth text is its core job. Learn the simple verification habits that keep you completely safe.

analogy.title: The Smooth Improv Actor
analogy.body: Think of an AI like a brilliantly eloquent improv actor on stage. If someone shouts "Tell us about the 1842 Treaty of Bluebell!", the actor refuses to freeze in silence—they smoothly invent an ambassador’s name, a cozy town, and a realistic clause that fits the rhythm of a history book. It sounds 100% confident even though none of it happened.

sections.heading: Why hallucinations happen in the first place
sections.body:
Because an LLM generates words by asking "What token looks most likely to come next?", its training rewards fluent, helpful-sounding answers. When you ask about something rare, hyper-specific, or brand new—like an obscure book citation, a small local restaurant’s hours, or a software feature released yesterday—the model may not have exact facts stored in its weights.

Instead of stopping cold, it fills the blank with whatever looks statistically right: a realistic author name, a plausible URL, or a convincing phone number. Researchers call this a **hallucination**.

callout.title: High-risk spots where AI hallucinates most
callout.body: Always double-check: exact legal/medical claims, academic citations and page numbers, live prices or store hours, exact quotes, and obscure biographical dates.

sections.heading: Grounding: turning a closed-book guess into an open-book check
sections.body:
The single best antidote to hallucinations is **grounding**—putting the real source material right onto the AI’s desk instead of asking it to recall from memory.

Rather than asking "What is my company’s refund policy?", paste the public refund policy text into the prompt and ask: *"Using ONLY the policy pasted below, answer the customer’s question and quote the exact sentence. If the policy does not say, reply: Not covered in the document."* Giving the AI explicit permission to say "I do not know" cuts guesswork dramatically—just remember to **redact private personal IDs, passwords, API keys, or confidential secrets** before pasting documents into any cloud chat.

callout.title: The "Quote the source" prompt pattern
callout.body: Add this line whenever summarizing non-sensitive PDFs, public policies, or articles: "Only use facts explicitly stated in the text above. Cite the exact heading or line for every claim, and flag anything missing."

sections.heading: A 30-second verification checklist for everyday life
sections.body:
You do not need to be paranoid about AI—just treat it like a sharp, fast intern whose work you glance over before signing your name:

1. **Check high-stakes facts at the source**: Click links, open the official site, or check the original document for numbers, dates, and medical/legal advice.
2. **Verify code by running it**: Never assume code works because it looks neat—run it and test the buttons!
3. **Ask AI to critique itself**: Prompting "List any assumptions you made or places where you might be uncertain" often catches shaky spots right away.

callout.title: Safe mental model
callout.body: Trust AI for drafts, structure, explanations, and starting points. Verify AI for facts, numbers, links, and final decisions—and never paste passwords or API keys into prompts.

keyTakeaways: A hallucination is a fluent, confident-sounding invention produced because LLMs optimize for plausible text patterns.
Grounding—pasting non-sensitive source documents or enabling live web search—turns risky memory guesses into verifiable open-book answers.
Give AI explicit permission to say "I don’t know," redact private secrets before pasting, and verify high-stakes facts before relying on them.

quiz.question: What is the most effective way to reduce hallucinations when asking AI about a specific clause in your apartment lease?
options: Paste the redacted lease text and ask it to quote the exact clause or say if missing.
Add a system rule warning the model to never guess wrong.
Lower temperature to 0.0 so it only outputs verified legal facts.
Ask three times in separate chats and trust the majority answer.
quiz.explanation: Grounding places the real (redacted) document on the AI’s working desk so it quotes actual clauses instead of guessing generic lease terms from memory.

quiz.question: If an AI writes a detailed citation with an author name, journal title, and publication year, that guarantees the paper actually exists.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Citations are one of the most famous places LLMs hallucinate—they know exactly what a realistic citation looks like and can assemble convincing fake ones unless verified.

quiz.question: Jordan asks an AI (without web search): "What time does the new cafe on Oak Street close tonight?" and drives over based on its confident "9:00 PM" reply. What went wrong?
options: He should have raised temperature to 0.8 so the model checked wider local business listings.
The model only stores store hours for major national chains unless you give it your zip code.
His prompt lacked a system prompt specifying the local time zone for the closing hour.
Ungrounded models guess plausible closing hours from patterns instead of checking live info.
quiz.explanation: Local live facts like business hours are classic hallucination territory when ungrounded. Always check live sources (or a search-grounded tool) for current real-world details.

masteryCheck.title: Unit 2 Mastery Check
masteryCheck.subtitle: Apply tokens, context hygiene, temperature, and grounding to four realistic situations.

questions.question: You have been brainstorming a holiday trip for 60 messages and now need an AI to draft a formal job cover letter. What is the smartest move?
options: Stay in the same thread so the AI warms up faster from all the previous tokens.
Raise temperature to 1.0 inside the travel thread so it ignores the trip details.
Start a fresh chat so old travel messages do not clutter context.
Paste "Forget everything above" three times in capital letters before your prompt.
questions.explanation: Opening a fresh chat clears unrelated messages off the working desk, preventing context distraction, lower quality, and wasted tokens.

questions.question: A team sets `temperature = 0` on an ungrounded customer-support bot and tells management: "Now the AI cannot hallucinate wrong return policies." What is wrong with that claim?
options: Temperature 0 only makes outputs repeatable; ungrounded models can still guess wrong.
Temperature 0 disables the tokenizer so replies shrink to one word.
Customer-support bots require temperature 0.9 to read pasted policy documents accurately.
Lowering temperature forces the chat wrapper to turn off live web search automatically.
questions.explanation: Temperature controls randomness, not truth. Without grounding the model in the real return policy text, temperature 0 simply makes its guesses consistent.

questions.question: You want an AI to extract warranty exclusions from a 12-page appliance manual PDF without guessing. Which prompt strategy works best?
options: Ask from memory first, then attach the PDF only if uncertain.
Attach the manual, ask it to answer strictly from that text, and cite exact headings.
Tell it to invent plausible terms whenever a section is tricky.
Ask for a creative story summarizing the manual at high temperature so nothing feels dry.
questions.explanation: Grounding with the real document, constraining answers to the pasted text, requiring citations, and allowing "not stated" sharply reduces hallucinations.

questions.question: Two messages have the exact same character count on screen: one is plain English prose, and the other mixes emojis, URLs, and non-English script. Which statement is accurate?
options: Both messages always use identical tokens because characters map 1-to-1.
Plain English costs more tokens because common words split per letter.
Token count depends only on spaces, so emojis add zero tokens.
The emoji, URL, and non-English message will usually consume noticeably more tokens.
questions.explanation: Tokenizers pack common English words into single tokens, while emojis, dense URLs, and many non-English scripts frequently split into 2–4 tokens each.

modules.title: AI Credits, Pricing & API Keys
modules.subtitle: Demystify subscriptions vs. pay-as-you-go credits, API key hygiene, real billing safeguards, and free local AI.

chapters.title: Chat Subscriptions vs. Pay-As-You-Go AI Credits
chapters.summary: Paying $20/month for ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro is completely separate from developer API billing. Learn how prepaid credits, postpaid cloud billing, and spending safeguards really work.

analogy.title: The All-You-Can-Eat Buffet vs. The Prepaid Coffee Card
analogy.body: A monthly chat subscription (like ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, or Gemini plans) is an all-you-can-eat buffet: pay one flat fee per month and eat inside the provider’s app (with fair-use pauses if you sprint too fast). Pay-as-you-go API billing is metered per cup: you pay for the exact tokens your apps or tools consume.

sections.heading: Why two separate billing systems exist
sections.body:
One of the #1 confusions for beginners happens right here: *"I already pay $20/month for Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus—why is this developer console asking me to add API billing?"*

Consumer chat apps and developer APIs are billed separately at almost every AI company. Your $20/month subscription covers chatting inside their polished website and mobile app (plus select bundled tools depending on your plan). Meanwhile, **API billing** pays for raw programmatic access through their API—the pipe that lets outside tools, automations, and backends talk directly to the model.

callout.title: Myth Buster: "Using the API is expensive and only for big tech companies"
callout.body: For light or medium builders, pay-as-you-go API usage is often MUCH cheaper than a $20/month subscription. Five dollars of credits on a fast model can fund hundreds—or thousands—of small requests.

sections.heading: When a subscription wins vs. when API billing wins
sections.body:
Choose a **monthly chat subscription** when:
• You chat casually every day in the browser or phone app.
• You want zero setup, built-in web search, voice mode, and predictable flat monthly pricing.

Choose **pay-as-you-go API billing** when:
• You use AI sporadically and do not want a recurring $20 bill.
• You want to plug AI into your own backends, automations, or trusted local developer tools.
• You want freedom to swap between Gemini, Claude, and GPT as needed.

callout.title: Prepaid credits vs. postpaid cloud billing—know the difference!
callout.body: Anthropic Console and OpenAI Platform let you load a small prepaid balance ($5) with **auto-reload turned OFF** (plus workspace monthly limits). By contrast, **Google Cloud / paid Gemini API is postpaid**: Google Cloud budget alerts only email you and **do NOT stop spending**! Stay on free tiers while learning, or set strict **API request quotas** alongside alerts.

sections.heading: Watch out for "wrapped" credit markup in third-party apps
sections.body: Many trendy AI websites charge $29/month for "500 AI credits" that call the exact same Gemini, Claude, or OpenAI APIs costing them a fraction of that behind the scenes. Paying for convenience is fine when a tool saves real hours—just compare its price against wholesale token rates so you choose with open eyes.

callout.title: Real-world cost perspective (illustrative rates)
callout.body: Sending a 500-word question and receiving a 500-word answer uses roughly 1,400 total tokens. On a fast budget model priced around $0.15/1M input and $0.60/1M output, that exchange costs well under a tenth of a single US cent.

keyTakeaways: Monthly chat subscriptions (flat fee inside the provider’s own app) and developer API billing (metered per token) are separate systems.
Prepaid balances with auto-reload OFF (like OpenAI and Anthropic) behave differently from postpaid cloud billing (like Google Cloud), where budget alerts alone do NOT stop charges.
Combine prepaid balances (auto-reload OFF), strict API rate/daily quotas, and small code limits to prevent surprise bills.

quiz.question: How does pay-as-you-go AI API billing typically calculate what you owe?
options: By counting how many hours your API key stays active in your developer dashboard.
By charging a fixed minimum monthly platform fee plus a flat rate per chat session.
By charging more whenever you switch between mobile apps and desktop browsers.
By metering the input and output tokens your requests use.
quiz.explanation: API billing is metered directly by token count (usually quoted per million input and output tokens), so idle time costs $0 and short prompts cost fractions of a cent.

quiz.question: Paying $20/month for a consumer chat website automatically includes unlimited free API credits for external apps you build.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Consumer web/mobile chat subscriptions and developer API billing are separate systems at major AI providers.

quiz.question: Rohan sets a $5 budget alert on his postpaid Google Cloud billing account and assumes Google will automatically shut off his Gemini API requests at $5.00. What did he misunderstand?
options: Google Cloud budget alerts require a $50 minimum first.
Postpaid cloud billing applies only to open-weights models and never affects hosted APIs.
Cloud budget alerts notify you without halting spend—you also need strict API quotas.
Budget alerts automatically cap output tokens while still charging full price for input tokens.
quiz.explanation: On postpaid cloud billing like Google Cloud, budget alerts only send notifications—they do NOT cut off API traffic. Pair alerts with tight API quotas or use prepaid credits with auto-reload OFF.

chapters.title: What Is an API & an API Key? (The Waiter and the Pass)
chapters.summary: An API is a clean digital doorway for software to talk to software, and an API key is the secret credential proving which project and billing account placed the order.

analogy.title: The Restaurant Waiter and Your Scoped Tab Card
analogy.body: Imagine dining at a restaurant. Your app does not wander straight into the kitchen (the AI server farm). Instead, it hands a structured order slip to the waiter (the API), who carries it to the kitchen and brings the reply back. Your API key is the secret card linked to a specific project tab—so you only hand out scoped cards with tight limits.

sections.heading: What actually happens during an AI API call
sections.body:
The acronym **API** (Application Programming Interface) is simply a predictable `https://` URL that accepts a neatly structured text package (usually JSON) and returns a structured answer.

Whenever a backend server or trusted local tool calls Claude, Gemini, or OpenAI, three things travel over an encrypted connection:

1. **The destination URL** (which AI endpoint to call)
2. **The auth header carrying your API key** (proving which account/project is ordering)
3. **The JSON body** (which model you want, your instructions, and your prompt)

A moment later, the server sends back the reply text plus exact token counts.

callout.title: Anatomy of an API call in 3 lines
callout.body:
• **URL**: `https://api.provider.com/v1/messages`
• **Header**: `Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY` (loaded from a server secret, never hardcoded!)
• **Body**: `{ "model": "fast-tier", "max_tokens": 300, "prompt": "Explain photosynthesis in 2 sentences" }`

sections.heading: Scoping keys and thinking carefully about BYOK
sections.body:
When you click **"Create API Key"** in a provider console, it generates a random secret string (`sk-...` or `AIza...`) and shows it **only once**. Save it straight into a password manager or OS keychain—never in sticky notes, screenshots, or chat threads.

Some local developer tools support **BYOK (Bring Your Own Key)** so you pay wholesale token rates instead of a markup. Before pasting a key into ANY third-party app, verify you trust its publisher, never paste an org-wide admin key, and mint a **dedicated, least-privilege key scoped to one project** (with minimum model permissions and tight spend/rate limits).

callout.title: Never paste live API keys into AI chats or untrusted web pages
callout.body: Pasting your real key into an untrusted web app’s "BYOK settings" box hands that site your billing access—and pasting a key into an AI chat prompt exposes it in conversation logs!

sections.heading: Create per-project keys, rotate them, and revoke fast
sections.body:
Good news: an API key is replaceable! Create separate labeled keys for each project (such as `recipe-backend-dev` and `notes-cli`), give each key only the permissions it actually needs, and revoke keys you stop using.

If you ever suspect a key leaked, click **Revoke / Delete** immediately in the provider console to shut it off worldwide, check your usage log for unauthorized calls, and mint a fresh replacement.

callout.title: Least privilege beats one master key
callout.body: If you reuse one admin-level key across five experiments and one experiment leaks, all five break when you revoke it—and an attacker gets broad account access. One scoped key per project keeps blast radius tiny.

keyTakeaways: An API is a structured HTTPS doorway that sends a model name and prompt and returns structured text plus token counts.
Mint one dedicated, least-privilege API key per project—never reuse an org-wide admin key or paste keys into untrusted web apps or AI prompts.
Store keys in a password manager and revoke any suspected leak immediately before checking billing logs.

quiz.question: Why should you create a separate, minimally scoped API key for each project instead of reusing one organization-wide admin key?
options: Providers block requests from one key across multiple days.
Reusing one key disables HTTPS on the request headers.
It limits the blast radius if one key leaks and lets you revoke it cleanly.
Each separate key unlocks a larger context window and faster token streaming speed.
quiz.explanation: Scoped, per-project keys follow least privilege: if one project leaks, attackers cannot touch unrelated projects or admin settings, and revoking it breaks nothing else.

quiz.question: If you accidentally share an API key in a screenshot, you have to delete your entire account because API keys can never be revoked.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! You can revoke (delete) a single compromised API key in seconds from your provider’s dashboard, audit usage, and immediately generate a fresh replacement.

quiz.question: Jamie pastes a live error snippet including `Authorization: Bearer sk-proj-9482a...` into a public forum AND into a consumer AI chat to debug it. What is the critical error?
options: He exposed a live credential that bots scrape in seconds—he must redact keys and revoke this one now.
He used `Bearer` instead of `Basic` authentication, which triggers an automatic account lock.
API error messages cannot be shared on forums even after replacing the key with a placeholder.
He sent the key inside a header instead of embedding it directly inside the public URL path.
quiz.explanation: Never share live keys in forums, screenshots, or AI chats. Replace them with `YOUR_API_KEY_HERE` before asking for help—and if a live key ever slips out, revoke it immediately.

chapters.title: Keeping API Keys Safe: `.env` Truths, Frontends & Limits
chapters.summary: A `.env` file is useful—not magic armor. Learn the real security rules pros follow: keep keys off frontends, understand what `.env` and `.gitignore` actually protect, and layer your cost limits.

analogy.title: The Separate Envelope Beside Your Public Blueprints
analogy.body: Imagine publishing blueprints of your house online. You never write your alarm code on the blueprint—you keep it in a separate envelope (`.env`). That keeps the code out of public copies, yet remember: a paper envelope is NOT a locked vault! Anyone standing at your desk—or any script given folder access—can still read it.

sections.heading: Golden Rule #1: Never put secret API keys in frontend/client code
sections.body:
The #1 beginner mistake is putting an API key inside browser HTML or JavaScript—or thinking a `.env` variable makes frontend code safe. **Anything delivered to a user’s browser is public**: visitors can open Inspect -> Network and read your key in seconds.

Watch out for frontend build-tool traps too: variables prefixed like `VITE_*` or `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` are bundled straight into public browser JavaScript even though they started inside `.env`! If a public web app calls YOUR paid AI key, route requests through a **backend server** where the key stays server-side.

callout.title: The 60-second bot sweep
callout.body: Automated bots scan public GitHub repos and web bundles continuously and can abuse a leaked key in under a minute. If a secret ever leaks, **revoke it first**, then clean up your files.

sections.heading: Golden Rule #2: What `.env` and `.gitignore` do—and do NOT do
sections.body:
Using `.env` alongside `.gitignore` separates local server secrets from shared code, as long as you know their real boundaries:

• **`.env` is plain, unencrypted text on disk**: It keeps secrets out of source code, NOT hidden from malicious scripts, zip backups, or AI agents reading your folder.
• **`.gitignore` only ignores UNTRACKED files**: Add `.env` to `.gitignore` *before* your first `git add`. If you already committed `.env` once, adding `.gitignore` later does NOT erase it from Git history!
• **Share `.env.example` instead**: Commit a harmless template like `OPENAI_API_KEY=your-key-here` with zero real values.

callout.title: Safe local hygiene before sharing code
callout.body: Run local deterministic checks (`git status`, `git diff`, `git grep`, or a secret scanner like `gitleaks` / GitHub Push Protection) and exclude `.env` from AI agent reads—never ask a cloud AI to open `.env` or paste live secrets into a prompt!

sections.heading: Golden Rule #3: Layer your spending controls—never rely on one switch
sections.body:
Billing safeguards work best in layers because provider metering can lag by several minutes during fast loops:

1. **Prepaid balance + auto-reload OFF** (where offered, such as OpenAI/Anthropic) plus workspace monthly spend limits.
2. **Hard API request/token quotas** (essential on postpaid Google Cloud, where budget alerts do NOT stop spend!).
3. **Code-level seatbelts**: set sensible `max_tokens` limits and cap retry loops in your own code so a bug stops after 3 tries instead of 3,000.

callout.title: Three checks before any first API test
callout.body: 1) Scoped project key stored outside frontend code? 2) `.env` in `.gitignore` before `git add`? 3) Auto-reload OFF and/or tight API request quota active?

keyTakeaways: Never put secret API keys in HTML, browser JavaScript, `localStorage`, or frontend-exposed env vars (`VITE_*` / `NEXT_PUBLIC_*`)—keep paid keys on a backend server.
`.env` is unencrypted plain text on disk, and `.gitignore` only protects untracked files—never let cloud AI read `.env`, and revoke immediately if a key ever touches Git history.
Layer cost safety: prepaid credits with auto-reload OFF, strict API quotas (especially on postpaid cloud billing), and code-level `max_tokens` / loop caps.

quiz.question: A developer stores `VITE_OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...` inside a git-ignored `.env` file and reads it directly in a public React browser app. Is the key safe from visitors?
options: Yes, because `.gitignore` encrypts the variable before the hosting server builds the app.
No—frontend build tools bundle `VITE_*` values straight into public browser code.
Yes, as long as the website runs over HTTPS and does not print the key on screen.
No, only because Vite requires keys to be stored in `localStorage` instead of `.env`.
quiz.explanation: Putting a secret in `.env` does NOT protect it if frontend code reads it! Variables exposed to the browser bundle can be inspected by any visitor. Keep paid keys strictly on a backend.

quiz.question: A `.env` file automatically encrypts your API keys on disk so no local program or AI agent with folder access can read them.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! `.env` is ordinary unencrypted plain text. It separates secrets from Git commits when properly git-ignored, but you must still keep it out of backups, public deploys, and cloud AI prompts.

quiz.question: Neha accidentally committed `.env` with her live API key to a public GitHub repo. She adds `.env` to `.gitignore`, deletes the key in a new commit, and stops there. What critical step did she skip?
options: She forgot to rename `.env` to `.env.secret` so GitHub’s servers recognize it as private.
She needed to ask a cloud AI chatbot to inspect her `.env` file to confirm the format.
Git history still holds the old commit and bots may already have the key—she must revoke it immediately.
She should have moved the key into `script.js` temporarily while rewriting `.gitignore`.
quiz.explanation: Adding `.gitignore` or making a follow-up commit never erases an already-exposed secret from Git history or scraper bots. Revoke and rotate the leaked key immediately first!

chapters.title: Reading Token Pricing & Free Local Models Like Ollama
chapters.summary: AI pricing tables look cryptic until you learn one trick: reading "per 1M tokens" and distinguishing input vs. output costs. Plus, learn how open-weights tools like Ollama run real AI locally for $0.

analogy.title: Wholesale Rice Pricing vs. Growing Herbs on Your Windowsill
analogy.body: Seeing "$3 per million tokens" is like seeing a wholesaler quote "$10 per metric ton of rice." You are not buying a whole ton for dinner—your single bowl costs less than a penny! And running a local model like Ollama is like keeping a basil pot on your windowsill: once set up, every leaf is free and offline.

sections.heading: How to read an AI pricing table in 15 seconds
sections.body:
Open any provider’s pricing page and you will see two numbers per model—for example, **$0.30 / 1M input tokens** and **$1.20 / 1M output tokens** (prices change over time, so always check the provider’s live page).

• **Input tokens** are everything you send (system prompt, chat history, pasted context).
• **Output tokens** are the fresh tokens the model writes back. Output typically costs 3× to 5× more because generating tokens sequentially requires heavier compute than reading input in parallel.

Quick mental math: divide any "per 1M" rate by **1,000** to get the cost per 1,000 tokens (~750 words). So $3 per 1M tokens is **$0.003** (three tenths of a cent) per 750 words.

callout.title: Worked example: how far $5 actually stretches
callout.body: At an illustrative fast-model rate ($0.15/1M input, $0.60/1M output), a 1,000-token prompt + 500-token reply costs `0.00015 + 0.00030 = $0.00045`—meaning $5 buys roughly **11,000 exchanges**. Even at a heavier tier ($3 input / $15 output), $5 still covers hundreds of rich chats.

sections.heading: Three quiet ways bills grow faster than expected
sections.body:
Because per-call prices are tiny, beginners usually spend pennies—except in three sneaky situations:

1. **Huge repeating chats**: Re-sending a 50-page document on every back-and-forth turn multiplies input tokens fast (even with prompt caching discounts).
2. **Runaway loops**: An automated script calling an API in a tight error loop—which is why loop limits in code, strict API quotas, and prepaid balances (auto-reload OFF) belong together, since billing caps can lag.
3. **Using flagship reasoning models for tiny tasks**: Use fast models for simple rewrites and save heavy thinkers for hard problems.

callout.title: Estimate any prompt cost in your head
callout.body: Take your rough word count × 1.33 to get tokens, divide by 1,000,000, and multiply by the model’s per-1M price. Knowing that 10-second check lets you spot expensive workflows immediately.

sections.heading: Free & Private: running local models with Ollama
sections.body:
What if you want zero cloud bills, zero API keys, and full offline privacy? Tools like **Ollama** make running open-weights models on your own computer straightforward.

After installing Ollama from its official site, one command—like `ollama run llama3.2` or `ollama run qwen2.5`—downloads a compact model onto your drive. From then on, it runs offline for $0! Compact 3B–8B models run smoothly on everyday laptops with 8–16 GB RAM, while larger models benefit from more memory or a dedicated GPU.

callout.title: Myth Buster: "Local models need a $10,000 server"
callout.body: Huge frontier models do need big servers, yet modern compact open-weights models (3B–14B parameters) run on ordinary consumer hardware and are genuinely useful for offline notes, study, and coding practice.

keyTakeaways: Divide a provider’s "per 1M tokens" rate by 1,000 to see the tiny cost per ~750 words—and remember output tokens cost more than input tokens.
Prevent bill surprises by keeping chats tidy, capping retry loops and `max_tokens` in code, and combining prepaid limits with strict API quotas.
Ollama lets you run compact open-weights models locally for $0 with full offline privacy and no cloud API key.

quiz.question: Why are output tokens almost always priced higher than input tokens on AI APIs?
options: Output tokens are checked against live search engines first.
Generating each new token sequentially takes more compute than reading input in parallel.
Providers add a separate fixed surcharge per punctuation mark.
Input tokens are compressed into a local cache on your phone while output runs in the cloud.
quiz.explanation: Reading your prompt happens in fast parallel batches, while generating each new output token sequentially requires much more compute per token—so output usually costs 3× to 5× more.

quiz.question: Running a local open-weights model through Ollama requires paying per-token API fees to OpenAI.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Ollama runs downloaded open-weights models directly on your own hardware—no cloud API key, no per-token bill, and it works completely offline.

quiz.question: Tariq sees a model priced at "$1.00 per 1M input tokens" and closes the tab thinking "I cannot afford $1 every time I send a message!" What did he misread?
options: 1M means one million tokens (~750k words), so a 500-word prompt costs under a tenth of a cent.
The $1.00 fee is a one-time setup charge that unlocks unlimited free prompts for a whole year.
Input tokens are only billed when you attach images or PDFs, whereas plain text prompts are free.
1M refers to one megabyte of internet bandwidth rather than the length of the conversation.
quiz.explanation: 1M = 1,000,000 tokens (roughly 750,000 words!). A normal 500-word message (~670 tokens) costs around $0.0007 at $1/1M—less than a tenth of a single cent.

masteryCheck.title: Unit 3 Mastery Check
masteryCheck.subtitle: Verify your judgment on API billing, key hygiene, frontend traps, and cost controls.

questions.question: A beginner switches Gemini API to a paid Google Cloud billing account and sets a "$5 monthly budget" thinking traffic will stop automatically at $5.00. What is the danger?
options: Google Cloud budget alerts only notify you—they do not stop API spend.
Google Cloud budgets automatically block input tokens while letting output tokens run free.
Monthly budgets on Google Cloud only take effect after your first $100 invoice clears.
Setting any budget alert immediately revokes all existing project API keys at midnight.
questions.explanation: Google Cloud Billing budgets send alerts only; they do NOT halt API traffic. Pair alerts with strict API request/token quotas, code loop caps, or use prepaid credit providers with auto-reload OFF.

questions.question: You want a public website where visitors click "Summarize" and call your paid AI API. Where must your secret API key live?
options: Inside a `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_KEY` variable in `.env` so the browser reads it safely.
Saved in `localStorage` so it stays out of HTML tags.
On a backend server that proxies requests, never in browser code.
Inside `styles.css` because visitors only check JS.
questions.explanation: Anything shipped to the browser—including `VITE_*`/`NEXT_PUBLIC_*` build vars and `localStorage`—is visible to visitors. Always keep paid keys server-side.

questions.question: Before pushing a side project to GitHub, you want to verify no API keys leaked into your code. Which approach is safest?
options: Paste your `.env` file into a web chatbot and ask it to search your repo for matching strings.
Run local `git status`, `git diff`, or `gitleaks` while keeping `.env` out of AI reads.
Push the repository first as public and check if any bots warn you within an hour.
Add `.env` to `.gitignore` after committing it and assume Git deletes past commits automatically.
questions.explanation: Deterministic local checks (`git status`, `git diff`, `git grep`, `gitleaks`, GitHub Push Protection) catch leaks reliably without exposing live `.env` secrets to cloud AI logs.

questions.question: Maya creates one organization-wide admin API key and pastes it into four different personal apps and a random free online "BYOK prompt tester." What best practice did she violate?
options: Admin keys cannot be used for inference unless you run Ollama at the same time.
BYOK tools require sharing your main account password alongside the API key header.
One key can only send requests to one model family per calendar month.
Always mint least-privilege project keys and never paste keys into untrusted web tools.
questions.explanation: Use dedicated, least-privilege keys scoped per project with tight limits, and never paste live keys into untrusted third-party web pages.

modules.title: AI Harnesses, Tools & Agents
modules.subtitle: Understand the leap from text-only chatbots to AI agents that read files, use tools, and ship real work safely.

chapters.title: Model vs. Harness: The Engine and the Car
chapters.summary: Why does the exact same AI model feel mediocre in one app and magical in another? The secret is the AI Harness—the software body wrapped around the model.

analogy.title: Same Engine, Completely Different Vehicles
analogy.body: Put the exact same powerful engine inside a bare go-kart with no headlights or steering wheel, and you barely leave the driveway. Put that exact same engine inside a finely tuned rally car with GPS, brakes, suspension, and a dashboard, and you conquer mountain roads. In AI, the LLM is the engine and the AI Harness is the car.

sections.heading: What an AI Harness actually does
sections.body:
You have probably heard builders compare Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, or Antigravity—even when those tools call the exact same underlying Claude, Gemini, or GPT models. Why do they feel so different?

Because an **AI Harness** is the complete orchestration program wrapped around the raw model. It controls:

• **What context enters the desk**: Loading the right project files and instructions.
• **Which tools exist**: Wiring up file reading, editing, terminal commands, or previews.
• **How steps repeat**: Running the model in a loop until checks actually pass.
• **Safety guardrails**: Enforcing least-privilege permissions, pausing for your approval before sensitive actions, and keeping context trimmed.

callout.title: Raw model vs. Harnessed agent on one task
callout.body: Ask a raw chatbot: "Fix the broken signup button in my project." It can only reply with guesses like "Try checking line 20 of your HTML." Ask the exact same model inside a coding harness: it opens your real files, spots the exact typo on line 47, proposes a surgical diff, runs the tests, and confirms the fix.

sections.heading: Why great harnesses matter just as much as smarter models
sections.body:
Imagine hiring a world-class architect—then locking them in a dark room with no measuring tape, no blueprints, and no phone. Even a genius cannot remodel your kitchen from inside a locked closet!

A well-built harness unlocks the room: it hands the model accurate blueprints (your files), a tape measure (tests and checks), and real permission boundaries so it cannot knock down a load-bearing wall without asking you first.

callout.title: Myth Buster: "Claude Code is a completely different LLM than Claude"
callout.body: Claude Code is a **harness** (specifically a command-line agent harness) powered by Claude models. Its power comes from pairing a strong model with file tools, diff reviews, permission controls, and smart context management.

sections.heading: What makes a beginner-friendly harness
sections.body:
When evaluating any AI tool, look past flashy demos and check four practical harness traits:

1. **Transparency**: Does it show you which files it read and what exact lines it wants to change?
2. **Permission controls**: Can you scope access tightly and say Yes or No before sensitive reads, edits, or commands run?
3. **Context hygiene**: Does it help keep long sessions tidy (like `/compact`)?
4. **Easy undo**: Does it pair smoothly with Git checkpoints so mistakes are easy to inspect and revert?

callout.title: Quick phone test: spot the harness layer
callout.body: Next time an AI tool impresses you by searching docs, running code, or showing diffs, ask yourself: "Which part was the raw LLM predicting text, and which part was the harness executing tools?"

keyTakeaways: The LLM is the engine; the AI Harness is the surrounding software (context loading, tools, execution loop, and permission controls) that turns raw intelligence into real action.
The exact same model can behave dramatically better inside a thoughtful harness than inside a plain text box.
Good harnesses give you clear visibility, explicit approval checkpoints, least-privilege permissions, and clean Git undo.

quiz.question: In the "Engine vs. Car" analogy, what role does the AI Harness play?
options: The surrounding vehicle—tools, context, loop, and safety controls.
The private training corpus used by the lab to tune model weights months earlier.
The billing account and token pricing sheet that tracks your monthly API usage.
The tokenizer dictionary that splits incoming English sentences into numeric IDs.
quiz.explanation: The LLM is the engine; the AI harness provides the tools, context management, execution loop, and safety controls that let the engine actually inspect files and finish tasks.

quiz.question: Two different AI coding apps using the exact same underlying model can produce very different results depending on the quality of their harness.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True! How a harness selects files, formats tool outputs, runs verification tests, and manages the context window makes a massive difference in real-world reliability.

quiz.question: Ben pastes "Fix my website’s broken navigation menu" into a plain web chatbot without sharing any files, and gets frustrated when it cannot edit his project directly. What is he missing?
options: Web chatbots need temperature 0.0 to reach local folders.
HTML files can only be modified by open-weights models running offline through Ollama.
He forgot to paste his personal API key into the web chat so it could unlock file permissions.
A plain web chat has no local file harness—he must share the code or use a local tool.
quiz.explanation: A plain browser chatbot is isolated from your local hard drive. To read and edit project files directly, the model needs a local harness with explicit file permissions!

chapters.title: Tool Calling, MCP & Real Permission Hygiene
chapters.summary: A language model only outputs text—so how does it read files or query services? Meet Tool Calling and MCP (Model Context Protocol), plus the real security risks of both reads and writes.

analogy.title: A Brain Passing Request Slips + USB-C Plugs
analogy.body: Imagine a strategist behind a glass wall. They cannot touch a keyboard directly, so they write a structured request slip: "TOOL: read_file, PATH: menu.html" and slide it under the glass. The harness checks permissions, fetches the file, and slides the contents back. MCP standardizes those tool plugs like USB-C so one connector works across many AI apps.

sections.heading: How tool calling works behind the curtain
sections.body:
Even inside the fanciest agent, an LLM NEVER directly clicks your mouse or modifies disk files. Instead, the harness gives the model a menu of permitted tools—such as `read_file`, `edit_file`, `search_web`, or `run_tests`.

When the model needs fresh information, it emits a structured **tool call** (a JSON slip like `{"tool": "read_file", "path": "index.html"}`). The harness catches that slip, checks your permission rules and approval settings, runs the tool, and hands the output back to the model.

callout.title: A three-second tool call in action
callout.body:
1. You ask: "How many rows are in sales.csv?"
2. Model emits tool call: `read_file("sales.csv")`
3. Harness checks permissions, reads the file, and returns 142 rows.
4. Model reports the real count instead of guessing.

sections.heading: The old cable mess—and why MCP was invented
sections.body:
Before 2024, connecting AI to external tools meant custom glue code for every single app—like the days when every phone needed its own proprietary charger.

**MCP (Model Context Protocol)** created one open standard: **"USB-C for AI."** Build an MCP server once for Notion, Google Drive, GitHub, or a database, and any MCP-compatible AI harness can plug straight into it using one shared protocol.

callout.title: Two halves of an MCP plug
callout.body: Your AI app is the **MCP Host/Client**. Each connector plugin (like a GitHub or Calendar integration) is a tiny **MCP Server**. Only install MCP servers from publishers you trust, because they execute code with whatever permissions you grant.

sections.heading: Why BOTH reads and writes need permission guardrails
sections.body:
A common myth is that read-only access is always completely safe. In reality, **both reads and writes carry real risks**:

• **Sensitive reads risk data exfiltration**: If an agent can read `.env`, `~/.ssh`, private emails, or tax files AND also has network or messaging tools, a single trick can leak those secrets out.
• **Untrusted content carries indirect prompt injection**: Reading a random web page, email, or GitHub issue can smuggle hidden instructions telling the agent to steal data or run commands!
• **Write/send actions have real-world impact**: Always apply **least privilege** (narrow scopes, exclude secret files, read-only database roles where possible) and keep **human approval ON** for writes, external messages, purchases, and shell commands—even in workflows you use regularly.

callout.title: Never treat reading untrusted docs or secret files as "harmless"
callout.body: Block agents from reading `.env` or credential folders, distrust instructions found inside external web pages/emails, and never grant blanket wildcard permissions (`*`) or auto-approve external actions.

keyTakeaways: Tool calling lets an LLM emit a structured request slip so its harness enforces permissions, executes the tool, and returns real output.
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is "USB-C for AI"—an open standard connecting AI harnesses to external tools and data.
