False
quiz.explanation: True! You do not have to memorize what every error means—knowing where to copy the exact clue turns you into an effective debugger immediately.

quiz.question: Kiran’s habit tracker shows `NaN` when he submits an empty streak, so he approves a sweeping 400-line AI rewrite that accidentally deletes his dark mode and delete buttons. What should he have done instead?
options: Approved it and asked AI to rebuild dark mode from memory.
Disabled `localStorage` so empty numbers never get saved.
Asked for a plain diagnosis and a minimal fix that leaves working features untouched.
Hidden the `NaN` label with CSS instead of validating input.
quiz.explanation: Minimal, targeted fixes protect everything that already works! Always review the diff and reject sweeping rewrites for tiny bugs.

chapters.title: Shipping Safely, Backups & Your Zero-to-One Roadmap
chapters.summary: You have gone from "What even is an LLM?" to understanding websites, stateful apps, and real security hygiene. Lock in your safe-shipping checklist, secret-free backups, and next build.

analogy.title: The Pilot’s Pre-Flight Card
analogy.body: Even airline captains with 20,000 flight hours still read a calm 6-item pre-flight card before every takeoff—not because they are beginners, because checklists turn safe habits into second nature. Keep your 6-item AI Builder checklist handy every time you ship something new!

sections.heading: Your 6-Point Safe-Shipping Pre-Flight Checklist
sections.body:
Before sharing ANY website or app with friends, coworkers, or the public internet, breeze through these six calm checks:

1. **Deterministic secrets sweep**: Verify zero API keys in HTML/JS using local checks (`git status`, `git diff`, `git grep`, or a secret scanner like `gitleaks` / GitHub Push Protection) and confirm `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
2. **Fresh-eyes test**: Open the app in a private/incognito window—does it start cleanly when `localStorage` is empty?
3. **Weird-input test**: Try tapping Submit with an empty box, a super long name, or a negative number—does it stay polite instead of crashing?
4. **Mobile check**: Does every button fit cleanly on a narrow phone screen?
5. **Clean backup & Git checkpoint**: Check `git status` first, then commit and back up without including `.env`.
6. **Billing & quota check**: If using any paid AI API on a backend, verify prepaid auto-reload is OFF, provider spend limits/alerts are set, and strict API request quotas + `max_tokens` caps are active (remembering postpaid cloud budget alerts alone do NOT stop spend!).

callout.title: Do NOT ask a cloud AI to "scan my folder for API keys"
callout.body: Letting an AI agent scan your folder can read `.env` and send live secrets into cloud context logs—and LLM scanning is not deterministic! Exclude `.env` from agent reads and use local tools (`git status`, `git grep`, `gitleaks`, GitHub Push Protection) for secrets checks.

sections.heading: Simple backups that never leak your secrets
sections.body:
Devices get lost and drives age, so keep clean backups:

• **Option A (Simple folder backup)**: Copy or zip your project folder into cloud storage—**excluding `.env` and credential files**, and storing API keys strictly in a password manager.
• **Option B (Builder Standard)**: Push your clean commits to a free **private GitHub repository** with GitHub Push Protection enabled. Now every milestone lives safely in the cloud with complete history!

callout.title: Check `.gitignore` and `git status` BEFORE your first `git push`
callout.body: Even in a private repo, keeping `.env` ignored builds rock-solid muscle memory so you never risk leaking keys if you collaborate or make a project public later.

sections.heading: Look how far you have come—and what to build next!
sections.body:
Take a second to appreciate what you now genuinely understand without hiding behind buzzwords: **LLMs & tokens**, **context windows & prompting**, **API billing, quotas & key hygiene**, **harnesses, tool calling, MCP & real permissions**, **AI CLIs & diffs**, **HTML/CSS/JS websites**, and **stateful apps with fearless debugging**.

The fastest way to cement everything? Pick ONE tiny real itch in your own life this week—a reading tracker, a freelance invoice estimator, a family recipe box, or a personal portfolio—write a 5-line Mini-Spec, and ship Version 1. Welcome to the builder club!

callout.title: 3 joyful starter projects to build next
callout.body:
• **Personal Link-in-Bio + Mini Portfolio**: Plain HTML/CSS deployed free on Netlify Drop.
• **Home Budget or Split-Bill Calculator**: Frontend JS + `localStorage` saved right to your phone home screen.
• **Automated Notes Helper**: Use a scoped AI CLI with a lean `CLAUDE.md` to tidy weekly meeting notes into crisp action lists.

keyTakeaways: Use local deterministic tools (`git status`, `git grep`, `gitleaks`, GitHub Push Protection)—never cloud AI prompts reading `.env`—for your pre-flight secrets sweep.
Back up projects cleanly via private GitHub repos or secret-free zips (storing real API keys only in a password manager), and layer billing quotas + prepaid limits.
Test empty states in incognito, weird inputs, and phone layouts before sharing Version 1.

quiz.question: Why is testing your finished web app inside a fresh Incognito / Private browser window such a smart pre-flight check?
options: Incognito mode automatically runs a secret scanner and strips out any accidental API keys.
It starts with empty `localStorage`, showing what a first-time user sees.
Private windows disable CSS animations so you can verify raw HTML accessibility scores.
Incognito mode simulates a backend database so multi-user syncing works without a server.
quiz.explanation: Your own browser often holds leftover test data in `localStorage`. Checking an Incognito window reveals the clean first-run experience every brand-new visitor gets!

quiz.question: Asking a cloud AI agent to scan your entire project folder (including `.env`) for leaked API keys is safer and more reliable than using local `git status`, `git grep`, or `gitleaks`.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: False! Letting a cloud agent read `.env` sends your live secrets into cloud context/logs, and LLM scans are not deterministic. Exclude `.env` from agent reads and use local secret scanners + GitHub Push Protection.

quiz.question: Meera finishes her Expense Splitter app, zips the entire folder (including `.env`) to a shared cloud folder, and deploys publicly with a test API key still inside `script.js`. What two safety mistakes did she make?
options: Leaving a key in public `script.js` and backing up `.env` inside a shared zip.
Testing her app in an incognito window and using plain CSS.
Adding `.env` to `.gitignore` and using a password manager.
Forgetting to buy a `.com` domain before checking how buttons fit on a narrow mobile screen.
quiz.explanation: Keep secret API keys completely out of public browser JS and exclude `.env` from zips and shared folders—store keys in a password manager and verify with local secret checks before shipping!

masteryCheck.title: Unit 7 Mastery Check
masteryCheck.subtitle: Prove you can scope MVPs, pick frontend vs. backend safely, debug from clues, and ship cleanly.

questions.question: Which project genuinely requires a backend server (not just browser `localStorage`)?
options: A single-user Pomodoro timer that saves your preferred work interval on one phone.
A public multi-user notes app with logins and calls to your paid AI API key.
A personal offline bill splitter used only at your table.
A private single-device flashcard deck storing study cards locally in your browser.
questions.explanation: Multi-user synced accounts and server-side paid API keys require a backend with proper access rules; single-user non-sensitive utilities work cleanly with `localStorage`.

questions.question: After you tap "Save Expense" with an empty amount, the total shows `NaN` and the console prints `TypeError at app.js:58`. What is the best debugging prompt?
options: Paste the exact steps and console error; ask for a 2-line diagnosis and minimal fix.
Tell the AI "it is broken" and approve a full 400-line rewrite of every file.
Ask the AI to hide `NaN` with white CSS text so users cannot notice the error.
Paste your live `.env` credentials alongside the error so the AI checks billing too.
questions.explanation: Exact reproduction steps + verbatim (secret-free) console clue + asking for a diagnosis and minimal targeted fix solves bugs cleanly without breaking working features.

questions.question: Before launching a small web app that connects to Supabase, a builder asks an AI CLI to read `.env` to verify keys and leaves database tables set to public read/write. What two security flaws exist?
options: Supabase databases only work with open-weights models and cannot store user habits.
Public read/write is safe as long as you test the app once inside an Incognito tab.
Letting a cloud AI read `.env` risks leaking secrets, and public DB tables expose user data.
Database access rules are unnecessary whenever `.env` is listed inside `.gitignore`.
questions.explanation: Never feed `.env` into cloud AI prompts (use local deterministic secret checks), and ALWAYS enforce backend database access rules like Row Level Security!

questions.question: You want to build a personal recipe box app with AI over a weekend. Which build plan gives the highest chance of shipping a working app?
options: Prompt all 14 features—accounts, grocery delivery, photo AI, and sharing—in one giant message.
Skip testing until the final hour so you can write code faster without interruptions.
Back up the entire folder including `.env` into a public GitHub repo before testing.
Define a 3-line item shape and ship one tested MVP slice at a time with Git commits.
questions.explanation: Clear data shapes, tiny testable MVP slices, and clean Git checkpoints after each working slice keep complexity small and bugs trivial to fix.

glossary.shortDef: Software that learns patterns from examples instead of following a rigid list of hand-written if/then rules.
glossary.analogy: Regular software is like a vending machine following fixed wiring; AI is like a seasoned chef who tasted ten thousand dishes and knows how flavors fit together.
glossary.example: Sorting spam emails by learning what shady messages usually look like, rather than blocking only one exact word.

glossary.shortDef: A type of AI trained on vast amounts of text and code to predict the most useful next chunk of text in a conversation.
glossary.analogy: Think of it as the world’s most well-read autocomplete—except it read so many books, manuals, and conversations that completing patterns looks like reasoning.
glossary.example: Claude, Gemini, GPT, Llama, and DeepSeek are all families of Large Language Models.

glossary.shortDef: The core mechanism inside an LLM: guessing the single most likely next word-piece, one piece at a time, until a full reply is formed.
glossary.analogy: Like finishing a friend’s sentence when they say "Peanut butter and ___"—except done thousands of times in a row while checking the whole page.
glossary.example: Given "The capital of Japan is", the model gives "Tokyo" a 99% probability and picks it as the next token.

glossary.shortDef: Billions of tuned numbers stored inside an AI model file that capture everything it learned during training.
glossary.analogy: Imagine a giant mixing board with billions of volume sliders; training adjusts every slider until the music sounds right, then freezes them in place.
glossary.example: A "70B" model has 70 billion parameters—larger files usually hold more knowledge, while smaller models run faster and cheaper.

glossary.shortDef: An AI model whose creators publish the trained weight files publicly so anyone can inspect, host, or run it on their own hardware.
glossary.analogy: Proprietary models are like eating at a restaurant with a secret recipe; open-weights models hand you the finished spice blend to cook at home.
glossary.example: Meta’s Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Mistral release open-weights models that you can run privately on a laptop.

glossary.shortDef: An AI model that can understand or create more than just plain text—such as images, screenshots, PDFs, audio, or video.
glossary.analogy: Instead of only reading letters mailed through a slot, a multimodal AI also has eyes to look at your photo and ears to hear your voice memo.
glossary.example: Taking a screenshot of a broken button on your website and pasting the image straight into Claude or Gemini to ask what looks off.

glossary.shortDef: Training is the expensive months-long study phase that builds a model; inference is the fast everyday act of asking the trained model a question.
glossary.analogy: Training is going to medical school for years; inference is a five-minute doctor visit where they apply what they already learned.
glossary.example: When you send a prompt and pay a fraction of a cent, you are paying for inference, not training.

glossary.shortDef: The user-friendly website or mobile app (like ChatGPT, Claude.ai, or Gemini) built around a raw model to add chat history, file uploads, and search.
glossary.analogy: The raw model is an engine sitting on a workshop stand; the chat app is the dashboard, steering wheel, and comfy seats around it.
glossary.example: When Claude.ai searches the web or shows an interactive preview card, that extra feature comes from the chat app, not just the raw model.

glossary.shortDef: A small chunk of text—roughly three-quarters of an English word—that AI actually reads, counts, and bills you for.
glossary.analogy: Think of tokens as Lego bricks of language: common words like "apple" are one brick, while rare or long words snap together from two or three smaller bricks.
glossary.example: "Unbelievable" might split into ["Un", "believ", "able"] (3 tokens), while a single emoji can take 2 to 4 tokens.

glossary.shortDef: The translator program that slices your text into numbered tokens before the AI sees it, and glues numbered tokens back into readable text for you.
glossary.analogy: Like a coat-check attendant who swaps every coat for a numbered ticket on the way in, and swaps tickets back for coats on the way out.
glossary.example: Because the tokenizer hands the AI chunks instead of individual letters, models sometimes miscount how many "r"s are in "strawberry".

glossary.shortDef: The maximum number of tokens an AI model can keep in active view at one time—including instructions, uploaded files, your chat history, and its reply.
glossary.analogy: It is the size of the AI’s working desk: once the desk is full of papers, adding a new page pushes the oldest page off the back edge.
glossary.example: A 200,000-token context window can hold roughly an entire 500-page book on the desk at once, though very cluttered desks still slow focus.

glossary.shortDef: The message, question, or instructions you give to an AI to tell it what you want.
glossary.analogy: Like giving directions to a bright new intern on day one: vague instructions get guesswork, while clear examples and goals get great work.
glossary.example: "Rewrite this apology email in 3 short sentences, warm and calm, without corporate buzzwords."

glossary.shortDef: Hidden top-level instructions placed before the conversation starts that define the AI’s role, tone, boundaries, and rules.
glossary.analogy: The employee handbook a hotel receptionist reads before opening the lobby doors—guests never see it, but it guides every answer.
glossary.example: "You are a patient cooking tutor. Always use metric measurements and warn beginners about hot oil."

glossary.shortDef: A dial (usually 0.0 to 1.0+) that controls how predictable or adventurous an AI is when picking its next token.
glossary.analogy: Low temperature is a careful accountant sticking strictly to the most likely answer; high temperature is a brainstorming poet willing to take wild creative detours.
glossary.example: Use low temperature (0.0–0.2) for summarizing invoices or fixing code, and higher temperature (0.7–0.9) for naming a coffee shop.

glossary.shortDef: When an AI invents a plausible-sounding fact, quote, citation, or code function that does not actually exist.
glossary.analogy: Like an improv actor who refuses to break character—even when they do not know the real fact, they smoothly make up something that fits the scene.
glossary.example: An AI inventing a realistic-looking court case name and date because the pattern "Smith v. State (2019)" sounds right.

glossary.shortDef: Giving an AI real source documents, web search results, or database records to base its answer on instead of relying purely on memorized patterns.
glossary.analogy: Switching from a closed-book exam (where guessing happens) to an open-book exam where you must point to the exact page number.
glossary.example: Pasting your actual lease PDF into the chat and asking, "Quote the exact clause about breaking the lease early."

glossary.shortDef: Prepaid or metered balance used to pay directly for the exact number of tokens you send and receive through an AI provider’s API.
glossary.analogy: A monthly chat subscription is an all-you-can-eat buffet; AI credits are a prepaid coffee card where you only pay for the exact cups you order.
glossary.example: Loading $5 of API credits can easily power hundreds of beginner chats or coding sessions on a fast model.

glossary.shortDef: A structured digital doorway that lets one piece of software send requests to another program—like your app talking directly to Claude or Gemini.
glossary.analogy: An API is the restaurant waiter: your app writes an order on a slip, the waiter carries it to the AI kitchen, and brings back the plated answer.
glossary.example: A backend server or trusted local tool sends a JSON message to an AI API endpoint and receives the model’s structured reply in seconds.

glossary.shortDef: A secret credential string (such as sk-...) that authenticates API requests and bills usage to your account—always scope it to one project with minimum permissions.
glossary.analogy: Like a company debit card tied to a specific budget: anyone who sees the number can spend your balance, so you issue scoped cards per project and revoke any card that leaks.
glossary.example: Storing your key in a password manager and server-side environment variables (or a git-ignored local `.env`), never inside public HTML, frontend JavaScript, screenshots, or AI chat prompts.

glossary.shortDef: A local plain-text configuration file that keeps secrets like API keys separate from source code—it is unencrypted on disk, so keep it out of Git, zip backups, and AI chat context.
glossary.analogy: A separate envelope tucked beside your blueprints rather than written on the blueprint itself—it keeps secrets out of public copies, though anyone who opens the envelope can read it.
glossary.example: Storing `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...` in `.env` for local server code while listing `.env` in `.gitignore` and never exposing it to frontend browser code.

glossary.shortDef: A plain-text checklist telling Git which untracked files—especially `.env` secret files—to ignore so they are never staged or pushed to a repository.
glossary.analogy: A "Do Not Pack" sticky note on your private folder before movers box up the room.
glossary.example: Adding `.env` to `.gitignore` before your first `git add` prevents accidental uploads—and if a key was ever committed earlier, revoke it immediately because `.gitignore` does not erase Git history.

glossary.shortDef: API providers charge per million tokens, usually pricing input tokens (what you send) much lower than output tokens (what the AI writes back).
glossary.analogy: Reading a customer’s two-page email takes seconds, while writing a thoughtful two-page reply takes much more effort—so writing costs more.
glossary.example: If a model costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, a typical 1,000-token exchange costs less than two cents.

glossary.shortDef: Safeguards that cap requests per minute/day (rate limits and quotas) or monthly spend (prepaid balances, workspace caps, and alerts)—noting that some cloud budgets only send alerts rather than stopping charges.
glossary.analogy: Combining a prepaid $5 coffee card (with auto-reload off) and a per-minute order limit so a runaway bug cannot quietly run up a big tab.
glossary.example: Keeping auto-reload OFF on prepaid Anthropic or OpenAI credits, setting workspace limits, and—on Google Cloud—pairing budget alerts with strict API request quotas.

glossary.shortDef: An open-weights AI model downloaded and run directly on your own computer with zero cloud fees and full offline privacy.
glossary.analogy: Instead of calling a delivery kitchen every time you want toast, you keep a toaster right on your own kitchen counter.
glossary.example: Installing Ollama and running `ollama run llama3.2` so your laptop answers questions offline for $0.

glossary.shortDef: The software shell wrapped around an LLM that manages its system prompt, context window, tool permissions, safety approvals, and step-by-step execution loop.
glossary.analogy: If the LLM is a powerful engine, the harness is the entire car—steering wheel, brakes, headlights, GPS, and seatbelts that make the engine actually drive somewhere useful.
glossary.example: Claude Code, Cursor, and Antigravity are AI harnesses: the same underlying model behaves dramatically better inside a well-built harness.

glossary.shortDef: An LLM inside a harness that can plan multiple steps, use tools to inspect or change the real world, check the results, and keep going until a goal is finished.
glossary.analogy: A chatbot is a consultant who only texts you advice; an agent is an assistant with keys to the workshop who opens the files, fixes the drawer, tests it, and shows you the result.
glossary.example: Asking an agent to fix a broken signup button—it reads your files, edits the bug, runs the tests, sees a pass, and reports back.

glossary.shortDef: The ability of an AI model to output a structured request asking its harness to run an action—such as reading a file, searching the web, or running a command.
glossary.analogy: A brain in a jar cannot turn a doorknob, so it passes a neatly written request slip to robotic hands that turn the knob and report what is behind the door.
glossary.example: Instead of guessing what is inside `index.html`, the model calls `read_file("index.html")` and receives the exact contents.

glossary.shortDef: An open standard that lets any AI harness plug into external tools and data sources (like Google Drive, Slack, browsers, or databases) using one universal format.
glossary.analogy: USB-C for AI: before USB-C, every gadget needed its own weird cable; with MCP, one standard plug connects your AI to hundreds of tools.
glossary.example: Adding a Notion or GitHub MCP server lets your AI assistant read your project tasks without you copy-pasting them manually.

glossary.shortDef: The repeating cycle an agent uses to solve multi-step tasks: think about the next step, call a tool, read the real output, and adjust until done.
glossary.analogy: How you assemble flat-pack furniture: look at the instructions, tighten one bolt, check if the leg wobbles, and move to the next step.
glossary.example: An agent edits CSS, checks the browser preview, notices the button text is cut off on mobile, adjusts padding, and verifies again.

glossary.shortDef: A safety checkpoint where an AI agent pauses for your explicit approval before editing files, running commands, sending external messages, or spending money—paired with least-privilege permissions.
glossary.analogy: A junior mechanic showing you the repair quote and waiting for your signature before ordering parts or touching the engine.
glossary.example: Reviewing a red-and-green diff or exact shell command and approving only the specific step needed rather than enabling blanket auto-approve.

glossary.shortDef: A plain-English markdown file in a project folder that shares preferences, folder layout, and workflow conventions with an AI tool every session (helpful guidance, not a hard security boundary).
glossary.analogy: A house-sitter’s welcome note taped to the fridge: "Water the fern on Tuesdays and follow the garden schedule"—handy reminders, while real locks still handle security.
glossary.example: Writing "Keep explanations jargon-free and always run npm test before saying you are finished" inside `CLAUDE.md`.

glossary.shortDef: Reusable instruction booklets you save once so an AI harness always follows specific standards (rules) or knows step-by-step playbooks for specialized tasks (skills).
glossary.analogy: Rules are everyday kitchen hygiene ("wash hands first"); skills are specific recipe cards you pull off the shelf only when baking sourdough.
glossary.example: A "Deploy Website" skill that reminds your AI agent of the exact 4 checks to run before publishing.

glossary.shortDef: A text-based window for talking directly to your computer’s operating system—doing the same things as clicking folders and buttons, just by typing short commands.
glossary.analogy: Clicking icons is pointing at pictures on a restaurant menu; the terminal is speaking directly to the kitchen in crisp shorthand.
glossary.example: Typing `ls` in the terminal lists the exact same files you see when opening your folder window.

glossary.shortDef: Any program you run by typing its name inside the terminal rather than clicking a graphical window icon.
glossary.analogy: Like texting a personal assistant quick commands instead of tapping through six screens of a mobile app.
glossary.example: `git`, `node`, `ollama`, and `claude` are all CLI tools.

glossary.shortDef: Anthropic’s terminal-based AI coding agent that lives right inside your project folder, reads your files, suggests edits with visual diffs, and runs commands with your approval.
glossary.analogy: Instead of emailing screenshots of your room to an interior designer, Claude Code walks right into the room with a tape measure and helps rearrange the furniture while you supervise.
glossary.example: Opening your `my-website` folder in the terminal, typing `claude`, and saying "Add a clean dark mode toggle to the top navigation bar."

glossary.shortDef: The exact folder your terminal is currently standing inside—every command or AI CLI you launch looks in this folder first.
glossary.analogy: Think of folders like rooms in a house: `pwd` asks "Which room am I standing in?", `ls` looks around the room, and `cd` walks into another room.
glossary.example: Running `cd ~/Marain-Projects/my-site` before starting `claude` so the AI edits your website instead of your whole home folder.

glossary.shortDef: A side-by-side or line-by-line highlight showing removed lines in red (`-`) and newly added lines in green (`+`) before or after an edit.
glossary.analogy: Track Changes in a Word or Google Doc—you do not have to reread the whole document, just the lines highlighted in red and green.
glossary.example: Reviewing a 4-line diff where Claude changed the button color from gray to emerald green before clicking Approve.

glossary.shortDef: A slash command in AI CLIs like Claude Code that summarizes a long, messy conversation into clean bullet notes to free up space in the context window.
glossary.analogy: Clearing twenty coffee-stained scratch pads off your desk and keeping one crisp sticky note with the decisions you actually care about.
glossary.example: Typing `/compact` after finishing the homepage header so the AI stays sharp and cheaper to run while building the contact form.

glossary.shortDef: A free time-machine system for project folders that tracks every change you make and lets you inspect diffs or roll back to an earlier working version.
glossary.analogy: Video game save slots for your files: before trying a bold experiment, you save the game so you can recover cleanly.
glossary.example: Running `git status` and `git diff` to see which files an AI edited before committing, or restoring a saved snapshot when an experiment goes sideways.

glossary.shortDef: A labeled snapshot of your project files saved into Git’s history at a moment when everything works nicely.
glossary.analogy: Taking a dated photograph of your Lego castle after finishing each tower, so if the roof collapses you know exactly how to rebuild.
glossary.example: Saving a commit labeled `"Homepage layout working on mobile"` before asking AI to add an interactive form.

glossary.shortDef: The skeleton of every webpage—plain text tags that define headings, paragraphs, images, links, and buttons.
glossary.analogy: If a website is a house, HTML is the wooden frame, walls, doors, and rooms before any paint or electricity goes in.
glossary.example:
`

Welcome to Bean & Book Cafe

` tells the browser to display a main title.

glossary.shortDef: The design rules that control how a website looks—colors, fonts, spacing, rounded corners, dark mode, and mobile layout.
glossary.analogy: The paint colors, lighting, furniture, and interior design that make the bare HTML house look inviting.
glossary.example: Setting a warm cream background, readable font size, and emerald rounded buttons in `styles.css`.

glossary.shortDef: The programming language built into every web browser that makes pages respond when you click buttons, type text, calculate totals, or save data.
glossary.analogy: The wiring and plumbing inside the house—flipping a switch turns on the light, and turning a faucet makes water flow.
glossary.example: Making a "Calculate Split" button actually divide a dinner bill and show each friend’s share instantly.

glossary.shortDef: A short, structured plain-English description of who a website or app is for, what sections or features it needs, and what vibe it should have—written before prompting AI.
glossary.analogy: Sketching a floor plan on a napkin before telling a carpenter to start cutting wood.
glossary.example: Listing audience, 4 page sections, color mood, and "must look clean on phones" in 8 bullet points before generating a site.

glossary.shortDef: Uploading your website or app files from your personal computer to a hosting server so anyone with a link can open it on the internet.
glossary.analogy: Moving a bakery’s test muffins out of your home kitchen and into a storefront window with a street address.
glossary.example: Dragging your finished website folder onto Netlify Drop or GitHub Pages to get a free public `https://` link in under a minute.

glossary.shortDef: All the live, changing information an app keeps track of right now—like which habits are checked off, what is in your cart, or whether dark mode is on.
glossary.analogy: A restaurant’s whiteboard of active orders: every time a dish is ordered or delivered, the whiteboard updates to reflect reality.
glossary.example: When you tap "+ Add Habit", the app updates its list in state and immediately redraws the screen to show the new row.

glossary.shortDef: Ways an app remembers data after reload—`localStorage` saves small non-sensitive data inside one browser, while a backend database stores shared data and protects secrets.
glossary.analogy: LocalStorage is a personal notebook in your own backpack (never put secrets in it); a cloud database with access rules is a shared vault that multiple devices can read safely.
glossary.example: A single-user Habit Tracker works great with `localStorage`; team sync, user accounts, or paid API keys require a backend with proper access rules.

glossary.shortDef: The smallest, simplest version of your app idea that actually solves the core problem—built first before adding fancy extras.
glossary.analogy: Building a sturdy skateboard that rolls today rather than waiting six months to finish a flying car.
glossary.example: Version 1 of an Expense Splitter just adds expenses and splits equally; user accounts and receipt scanning wait for Version 2.

glossary.shortDef: The browser or terminal’s behind-the-scenes diagnostic log where programs print exact clues (file name, line number, and reason) whenever something breaks.
glossary.analogy: The check-engine diagnostic code a mechanic plugs into your car—even if you cannot fix the engine yourself, handing the exact code to AI lets it spot the broken wire immediately.
glossary.example: Copying `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading "value") at app.js:42` and pasting it straight to your AI assistant.

glossary.shortDef: The frontend is everything users see and click on their screen; the backend is the behind-the-scenes server that safely handles logins, shared databases, and secret API keys.
glossary.analogy: The frontend is the dining room of a restaurant; the backend is the kitchen and supply vault where ingredients and secret recipes stay safe.
glossary.example: A personal portfolio needs only a frontend, while an app with user accounts and paid subscriptions also needs a backend.
